articles.title: The editor at a glance
articles.summary: Where everything is: the bar on top, the rails at the sides, the orientation cube, and the model in the middle.
articles.keywords: layout interface overview start beginner tour where bar rail cube toolbar menu ui screen window panel home first time lost find
articles.body:
The model is in the middle. Everything else sits at the edge and stays quiet until you reach for it.

![](image:layout)

1. **The top bar.** The house on the left goes back to your projects. Next to it is the workspace button, which reads Modeling to begin with, and then the name of the project: click the name to rename it. Export is on the right.
2. **The left rail.** Items at the top, then Sketch, File, Transform and Tools in the middle, then Section View and Measure at the bottom. Rest the pointer on the rail and the names appear.
3. **The orientation cube**, top right. Click a side to look from there.
4. **Quick settings**, the button at the bottom right. It opens one small panel with View, Display and Units & Grid as tabs across its top.

## The left rail

![](image:rail)

- **Items** opens the list of what the project is made of. See [items](doc:items).
- **Sketch** is a mode. The rail turns into the sketch tools until you press Finish Sketch. See [start a sketch](doc:start-a-sketch).
- **File** brings a file in: a part, a mesh, a drawing or a [picture](doc:reference-image). See [import](doc:import).
- **Transform** and **Tools** open a second column of commands beside the rail, each with its key. Transform holds Move/Rotate, Scale, Mirror and Pattern. Tools holds Chamfer/Fillet, Extrude, Shell, Hole, Revolve, Combine and Split. Press the same button again to put the column away.
- **Section View** and **Measure** look at the model without changing it. See [section view](doc:section-view) and [measure](doc:measure).

## Quick settings

- **View**: the standard views, Zoom to fit and the field of view. See [standard views](doc:standard-views).
- **Display**: Shaded, Wireframe or X-Ray, edges and axes, and the theme. See [Wireframe, X-Ray and Shaded](doc:display-modes).
- **Units & Grid**: the unit of length, and the grid: whether it is shown, its plane and whether a sketch snaps to it.

What holds in every workspace and not only for this model, such as the theme, is under a heading marked Every workspace. Visualize and Drawings have the same button, at the foot of the picture beside their own panel, with only the sections that apply there.

> Nothing is saved with a button. Every change is written to disk before it is applied, so closing the tab loses nothing. If something goes wrong, see [undo and redo](doc:undo-redo).

To move the camera, see [orbit, pan and zoom](doc:navigate).

layout.alt: The editor with a box in it, and the places the text names

rail.alt: The Tools column open beside the left rail

articles.title: Orbit, pan and zoom
articles.summary: Move the camera around the model with a mouse or a trackpad, the way the CAD you know does.
articles.keywords: orbit rotate pan zoom camera mouse trackpad scroll wheel pinch navigation gesture move view turn preset blender fusion solidworks onshape rhino sketchup inventor tumble spin
articles.body:
Orbit turns the model, pan slides it, zoom brings it closer or further away. Bezier starts with its own way of doing each (Native), and can follow another program instead.

## The default

- **Orbit**: right-drag, or two fingers on a trackpad.
- **Pan**: middle-drag, or Shift and right-drag, or Shift and two fingers.
- **Zoom**: the wheel, or a pinch.

You can turn all the way around the model, over the top and under the bottom, without having to turn back. When the hand stops, the model stops.

To look from exactly the front, the top or another side, use the orientation cube. See [standard views](doc:standard-views).

## Use the keys of another program

1. Open Settings and choose Interaction. See [open Settings](doc:open-settings).
2. Next to Navigate like, choose Native, Blender, Fusion 360, SolidWorks, Onshape, Rhino, SketchUp, Siemens NX, Alias or Inventor.
3. To change one action only, use the lists under Mouse. A changed action says Changed, and Reset All Mouse Bindings puts them all back to the preset.

![](image:settings)

## If the wheel does the wrong thing

A browser cannot tell a mouse wheel from a trackpad, so Bezier guesses. If the wheel turns the model when you meant to zoom, or two fingers zoom when you meant to orbit, say which you use: Settings, Interaction, Scrolling comes from, or Scrolling with under View in the quick settings. The switch Wheel zooms the other way reverses the wheel.

> To look straight at a face, see [square up to a face](doc:square-view).

settings.alt: Settings, Interaction, with Navigate like and the Mouse actions

articles.title: Projects, folders and the start page
articles.summary: Everything you have made is on the start page, on your machine, with the picture you last saw.
articles.keywords: projects start page home folder new rename delete move card library organise organize file open recent duplicate remove list
articles.body:
The start page is what opens first. Every project on this machine is a card with the last view you had of it, newest first.

![](image:start)

## The everyday steps

1. **New Project** is at the top right of the page. Ctrl or Cmd and N does the same while the start page is showing.
2. Click a card to open it. Click the house in the editor to come back.
3. **Rename**: click the name on a card, or the name of the project in the editor. Press Enter to keep it, Escape to leave it as it was.
4. **Folders**: press the folder button beside Folders in the sidebar, then drag cards onto the folder.
5. **Delete** asks once, then removes the project from this device.

## The card menu

Press the three dots on a card, or right-click anywhere on it.

![](image:menu)

- **Open**
- **Rename…**
- **Move to Folder…**: the same as dragging the card onto a folder.
- **Export…**: opens the project and points you to Export in the top bar. See [export](doc:export).
- **Delete**

Once you are connected for [collaboration](doc:collaboration), Share… is in the menu too.

## Folders

A project is in one folder at most, and All Projects always lists everything, wherever it is filed. Click a folder in the sidebar to see only its projects. Click the name of the open folder to rename it, or use its three dots for Rename… and Delete. Deleting a folder does not delete its projects: they go back to All Projects.

To move several projects at once, Shift-click or Cmd-click or Ctrl-click the cards, or drag a rectangle over empty space around them, then drag any one of them onto a folder. Escape clears the selection.

## Delete

Delete asks "Delete project?" and says the project will be permanently deleted from this device. This cannot be undone. Press Cancel if you are not sure.

> A new project you leave without doing anything is not kept.

To find a project among many, see [search](doc:search).

start.alt: The start page with a library of projects, a folder, and New Project

menu.alt: The menu of a project card

articles.title: Search everything from one field
articles.summary: One field on the start page finds projects, settings and wiki articles. ⌘K finds an article from anywhere.
articles.keywords: search find field projects settings docs wiki article operator slash quick filter look up where command k shortcut palette
articles.body:
Use the search field to find a project by name, a setting by what it does, or an article by what it explains.

1. The field is at the top of the sidebar on the start page. Press **/** to jump into it.
2. Type a word. Projects, settings and wiki articles that hold it appear together, under Results for what you typed.
3. Click a result. A project opens, a setting opens its page in Settings, an article opens in the wiki.

![](image:results)

Several words must all be found. A project is also found by the name of its folder.

## Look in one place only

Start with the place and a colon.

- **projects:** bracket looks only through project names.
- **settings:** theme looks only through Settings, and opens it, narrowed to what matches.

Spelled out, `project`, `setting`, `prefs` and `preferences` work too.

## On other pages

On the Learn and Community pages the words narrow what is on the page instead. Start with `projects:` to reach projects from there.

## To clear it

Press Escape in the field. If nothing matches, the page says so and reminds you of the two prefixes.

## Find an article from anywhere

Press Ctrl or Cmd and K, on the start page or inside a project. A search over the whole wiki opens on top of whatever is on screen. Type, move with the arrow keys and press Enter. Inside a project the article opens in a window floating beside the model. See [the wiki](doc:community).

> Search finds articles about [the editor](doc:editor-at-a-glance), [Settings](doc:open-settings) and everything else here. Look up words from the program you know: fillet, loft, constraint, pad, extrude.

results.alt: The search field with a word typed, and the projects, settings and articles found

articles.title: Modeling, Drawings, Visualize and Simulation
articles.summary: Four workspaces over the same model, switched from the top bar.
articles.keywords: workspace modeling design drawings visualize simulation switch mode render stress sheet change tab
articles.body:
A workspace is a way of looking at the one model you have: building it, testing it, showing it, drawing it. They share everything. A change made in Modeling is in the others at once.

1. Press the workspace button in the top bar, next to the house. It names the workspace you are in.
2. Choose one.

![](image:menu)

- **Modeling**: sketch, model and refine solids. This is where a project opens.
- **Simulation**: loads, supports, stress and topology. See [simulation](doc:simulation).
- **Visualize**: materials, studio lighting and renders. See [visualize](doc:visualize).
- **Drawings**: technical sheets, dimensions and vector exports. See [drawings](doc:drawings).

## By keyboard

Press Alt and Cmd (or Ctrl) with 1, 2, 3 or 4 for Modeling, Simulation, Visualize and Drawings, in the order of the menu. Escape closes the menu.

> Switching workspace changes the tools on screen. It does not change the model.

articles.title: Items: what the project is made of
articles.summary: A list of the bodies and sketches of the project, where you select, rename, hide and reopen them.
articles.keywords: items tree list bodies sketches filter rename hide show eye panel layer outliner browser feature tree model tree isolate folder
articles.body:
Items is the list of what is in the project: its bodies, its sketches, and any reference meshes and imported files. Use it to pick something that is hard to click, to hide what is in the way, and to get back into a sketch.

1. Press the layer button at the top left, or {{key:items}}. The list slides in beside the rail. Press it again to put it away.
2. Click a row to select it. A body is picked in the model too; a sketch opens its numbers on the right. Shift-click picks every row between the last one you clicked and this one; Cmd-click or Ctrl-click adds or removes one row.
3. Double-click a body's name to rename it. Enter keeps the name, Escape leaves it. Renaming can be undone.
4. The **eye** hides a body. It shows on the row under the pointer and on the selected row, and stays on anything hidden. Alt-click the eye to show that body alone.
5. The filter at the top, All Items to begin with, narrows the list to Sketches or to Bodies.
6. Drag the right edge of the panel to make it wider. Double-click the edge to set it back.

![](image:list)

## What the rows are

- **Bodies** each solid of the project. A file brought in with [import](doc:import) is a folder named after the file, holding the bodies it contained; click the folder to pick them all.
- **Sketches** each drawing. At the far end of a sketch row is the body it was built into. Once a sketch has been used it is no longer drawn in the model, and its row is dimmed with a struck eye. Click the row to bring it back.
- Hiding a body does not delete it. Hidden bodies stay in the list and come back with the eye.

## Reopen a sketch

Double-click a sketch row to draw in it again. See [change a sketch afterwards](doc:reopen-sketch).

![](image:filter)

> Change a number in a sketch and everything built from it is built again. See [variables](doc:variables) to name a number once and use it in many places.

list.alt: The Items list: two bodies, one hidden, and the sketches they were built from

articles.title: Sketching in five minutes
articles.summary: The whole path from an empty plane to a solid: draw, relate, size and extrude, with a plate and a hole.
articles.keywords: sketch sketching tutorial quick start beginner 2d profile draw dimension constrain extrude workflow first part plate hole overview how
articles.body:
A sketch is a flat drawing on a plane or on a face. You draw shapes in it, say how big they are, and pull an area of it into a solid. This page goes the whole way once, with a plate that has a hole in it.

## 1. Start

1. Click **Top** on the orientation cube, top right. The view squares up to the floor.
2. Press **Sketch** in the left rail. The rail turns into the sketch tools, and the plane you are looking at is the one you draw on.

More on planes and faces in [start a sketch](doc:start-a-sketch).

## 2. Draw

1. Press {{key:rectangle}}. Click one corner. Type **60**, press Tab, type **40**, press Enter. The rectangle is 60 by 40 millimetres, toward where the pointer is.
2. Press {{key:circle}}. Click inside the rectangle, move out, click again.
3. Click the number beside the circle and type **12**. Press Enter.

![](image:drawn)

Each tool is in [line](doc:line), [rectangle](doc:rectangle), [circle](doc:circle) and [arc](doc:arc). Escape puts the tool down.

## 3. Relate

A rectangle comes with its sides held horizontal and vertical. For anything else, pick the lines, and the Constraints bar offers what fits: Parallel, Perpendicular, Equal and the rest. See [constraints](doc:constraints).

## 4. Size

Every line and circle shows its size beside it. Click a number, type another and press Enter. Escape leaves a number as it was. See [exact sizes](doc:dimensions).

## 5. Extrude

1. Press **Finish Sketch**, or Enter.
2. Click inside the plate, outside the circle. The circle is a hole in it, so the area you click is the plate and not the disc. An arrow and a distance field appear.
3. Type **8** and press Enter. The plate stands up 8 millimetres, with the hole through it.

![](image:offer)

![](image:result)

Nothing is built until you give a distance. Escape takes the offer away. See [extrude](doc:extrude) for the direction and for adding to or cutting from a body.

## When something goes wrong

- A shape you did not mean: press {{key:undo}}. In a sketch it takes back the last thing drawn. See [undo and redo](doc:undo-redo).
- Nothing happens when you click inside a shape: the lines do not meet. A corner must be shared by two lines, not just close to each other. Draw to the point, or [trim](doc:trim) what overshoots.
- To change the sketch later, double-click it in Items. See [change a sketch afterwards](doc:reopen-sketch).

drawn.alt: A 60 by 40 rectangle with a 12 mm circle inside it, in a sketch

offer.alt: The plate clicked, with the arrow and the distance field of the extrude

result.alt: The finished plate with its hole

articles.title: Start a sketch
articles.summary: Choose a plane, or a face, and draw on it.
articles.keywords: sketch start begin plane face draw 2d profile finish plane choose xy xz yz front top right workplane datum new sketch
articles.body:
A sketch lives on a flat surface: one of the three planes through the origin, or a flat face of a body.

1. Press **Sketch** in the left rail. The rail turns into the sketch tools.
2. Say where to draw:
   - Click the plane to draw on: the floor, which is XY, or one of the two upright planes, XZ and YZ.
   - Or click a flat face of a body first, then press Sketch. The rail's top button then says On a face.
3. Draw. See [line](doc:line), [rectangle](doc:rectangle), [circle](doc:circle) and [arc](doc:arc).
4. Press **Finish Sketch**, or Enter. The rail comes back.

![](image:planes)

## The short way

- If you are looking along an axis when you press Sketch, for example after clicking Top on the cube, it opens on the plane facing you. No click needed.
- Press a tool's key, such as {{key:line}} or {{key:rectangle}}, outside a sketch. It starts one on the plane you are looking at. If the view is not square to a plane it says Choose a plane to sketch on first, and the tool is in your hand once you have.
- Press Sketch again, while sketching, to finish.

## On a face

![](image:face)

Only a flat face can be sketched on. A curved face says so. A sketch on a face follows it: if the face moves when you change an earlier step, the sketch moves with it. To bring the outline of the face into the sketch, see [project the edges of a face](doc:project-edges).

## A plane at an angle

Once a plane or face is chosen, a bar at the foot of the canvas holds three numbers for it: **Offset** moves it along its normal, **Tilt** turns it about its own horizontal axis and **Turn** about its upright one. XY tilted by 45 is a plane halfway between the floor and a wall. The grid lies on the plane you draw on, at whatever angle, so its cells are the ones snapping counts. The numbers are kept with the sketch and can be changed later in its bar.

## Every sketch is its own

Pressing Sketch always starts a new sketch. It does not go back into the last one. To draw in an old sketch, double-click it in Items. See [change a sketch afterwards](doc:reopen-sketch).

> The button at the top of the sketch rail reads Finish Sketch, and under it says which plane you are on: XY plane, On a face, or No active plane while you have not chosen one. An empty sketch is dropped when you leave it.

Back to [sketching in five minutes](doc:sketch).

planes.alt: The sketch tools in the rail, and the three planes to draw on

face.alt: A sketch started on the top face of a block

articles.title: Line
articles.summary: Draw straight lines one after another; a chain that closes becomes an area to extrude.
articles.keywords: line polyline segment draw sketch chain close dimension length straight edge angle snap
articles.body:
1. In a sketch, press {{key:line}}, or choose Line in the rail.
2. Click for each point. Each click starts the next line where the last one ended.
3. To close a shape, click the first point again. The lines join there, and the area fills in.
4. Press Escape to end the chain. Press it again to put the line tool down, and a third time to leave the sketch.
5. Click the length beside a line to type an exact size in millimetres, then press Enter.

![](image:chain)

## Type a length as you draw

While a line is stretching from the last point, type digits: 50 makes it 50 mm long. The pointer still decides the direction. Press Enter to place it, or click. Backspace takes the last digit away.

## Joining

A click within a millimetre or two of an existing point reuses that point, so the lines are joined and not just touching. That is what makes a closed shape: a shape whose corners are only close is not closed, and cannot be extruded. If Snap to grid is on, free clicks land on the grid. See [exact sizes](doc:dimensions).

A chain that closes is an area, and clicking inside it goes straight on to [Extrude](doc:extrude). For a line that guides and does not shape, see [centerline](doc:centerline) and [construction](doc:construction).

chain.alt: A triangle of three lines, closed, with their lengths

articles.title: Rectangle
articles.summary: Draw a rectangle from corner to corner or from its centre.
articles.keywords: rectangle box square sketch draw profile corner centre center diagonal two point width height rect
articles.body:
1. In a sketch, press {{key:rectangle}}, or choose Rectangle in the rail.
2. Choose how: **Diagonal** is corner to corner, **Center** is centre to corner. Open the choice with the small mark on the Rectangle button, or press the key again to switch between them.
3. Click once to start and once more to set the size.

![](image:variants)

## Type the size

After the first click, and without moving the pointer, type the length, press Tab, and type the width. Enter places the rectangle. Tab goes back and forth between the two, and Backspace takes a digit away.

![](image:typed)

The sizes you type stay as dimensions on the sides, and you can change them later: click a number and type another. See [exact sizes](doc:dimensions).

## What you get

A rectangle is four lines with their corners joined, two sides held horizontal and two held vertical. It stays a rectangle when you change a width. Because the corners are shared, it is a closed area at once.

Press Finish Sketch. Clicking inside the rectangle then goes straight on to [Extrude](doc:extrude). A rectangle drawn inside another is a hole in it. See [several shapes, holes and areas](doc:sketch-areas).

variants.alt: The two kinds of rectangle in the rail

typed.alt: A rectangle being drawn with its length typed in

articles.title: Circle
articles.summary: Draw a circle from its centre, and set its diameter.
articles.keywords: circle round diameter radius hole sketch draw disc cylinder ellipse centre center
articles.body:
1. In a sketch, press {{key:circle}}, or choose Circle in the rail.
2. Click the centre, then move out. The diameter shows beside the pointer, with the sign ⌀.
3. Click to set it.

![](image:diameter)

## Set the size

A circle stays editable. Click its diameter at any time, type another and press Enter.

You can also type while you draw: after the centre click, type a number and press Enter. The number is taken as the **radius**, in millimetres, while the label shows the diameter. Typing 20 gives a circle marked ⌀ 40. If you want to be sure of a diameter, draw the circle and then click the number beside it and type the diameter.

## Through three points

Circle's 3-point variant, beside Center in the rail, draws the circle through three clicks. Clicks on points already there stay on the circle.

## A circle inside a shape

A circle drawn inside a closed shape is a hole in it. Click the area around it to extrude the shape with the hole. See [several shapes, holes and areas](doc:sketch-areas). A circle alone is an area too: extruding it makes a cylinder.

A circle can be turned into a guide: see [construction](doc:construction).

diameter.alt: A circle with its diameter, ⌀, written beside it

articles.title: Arc
articles.summary: Draw a curved segment between two points.
articles.keywords: arc curve radius bend round sketch draw three point fillet curved side
articles.body:
1. In a sketch, press {{key:arc}}, or choose Arc in the rail.
2. Click the two ends of the arc.
3. Move to bend it. The radius shows, marked with R.
4. Click to set it.

![](image:arc)

An arc that closes against a line makes an area with a curved side, and extrudes as an exact curve.

## Joining

An end of an arc that you click near an existing point joins it, as a line does, so a line and an arc can close a shape. Click on the ends of a line you have drawn and the arc is built on it, as in the picture.

## From its centre, or along a line

Arc has three variants in the rail. **3-point** is the one above. **Center**: click the centre, then where the arc starts, then which way round to where it ends. **Tangent**: click the end of a line, then where the arc ends; it leaves the line along it and stays tangent to it.

## Rounding a corner instead

To round a corner between two lines that you have already drawn, use Fillet in the Constraints bar, not an arc. See [chamfer or fillet a corner](doc:sketch-corner).

arc.alt: A line, and an arc being bent between its ends, with its radius R

articles.title: Trim
articles.summary: Cut away the part of a line that reaches past where it should stop.
articles.keywords: trim cut extend overdrawn remove remainder sketch clean overshoot break split divide
articles.body:
Trim is for the line you drew a little too long. It removes the part that sticks out, up to the line it crosses.

1. Draw lines that cross, so that one reaches past the shape.
2. Press {{key:trim}}. Trim is lit in the rail.
3. Click the part that sticks out. It is removed up to the line it crosses.

![](image:before)

![](image:after)

Trim both ends of an overlong closing line and the shape is closed, with nothing left over.

## Extend and split

Trim has two more variants in the rail. **Extend**: click near the end of a line and it grows to the first line, circle or arc ahead of it; only a free end grows. **Split**: click along a line and it is cut in two there, the halves sharing the new point.

## Good to know

- Click the part you want gone, not the part you want to keep.
- Press Escape to put Trim down. To undo a trim, press {{key:undo}}.
- To remove a whole line, pick it and use [delete](doc:sketch-delete).

before.alt: Trim on, with a line reaching past the shape

after.alt: The same sketch after the overshoot was clicked

articles.title: Centerline
articles.summary: A line to measure and align against, that is never part of a shape.
articles.keywords: centerline centreline axis helper guide construction symmetry mirror axis dashed reference
articles.body:
A centerline is a guide. It is not part of any shape, and it is never extruded.

1. In a sketch, choose Centerline in the rail.
2. Click its points as you would for a line.

![](image:drawn)

A closed chain of centerlines encloses no area, so there is nothing to extrude. It is there to draw against: to snap to, to measure from, to hold a symmetry.

Centerline is the Line tool, drawing in construction. A centerline looks the same as any construction line, dashed. Press Escape to put the tool down.

> To turn a line you already drew into a guide, see [construction](doc:construction).

drawn.alt: A rectangle with a centerline drawn through it

articles.title: Construction
articles.summary: Turn a line into a guide, drawn dashed, that shapes nothing.
articles.keywords: construction guide dashed helper toggle reference line geometry non-printing switch normal
articles.body:
1. In a sketch, click a line to pick it. Shift-click to pick more.
2. Choose Construction in the rail.

The line is drawn dashed from then on, and it no longer takes part in any shape. A side of a rectangle that you switch to construction opens the rectangle, so it no longer encloses an area.

![](image:dashed)

Choose Construction again on the same lines to turn them back into ordinary lines. With a mix of both picked, they all become construction first.

It works on arcs and circles too, for a circle that only places the holes on.

See also [centerline](doc:centerline), which draws guides from the start.

dashed.alt: The top side of a rectangle, switched to construction

articles.title: Project the edges of a face
articles.summary: Bring the outline of a face into the sketch you are drawing on it.
articles.keywords: project edges face outline copy sketch reuse trace convert entities offset silhouette boundary
articles.body:
Use this to build on something that exists: a boss on a face, a pocket inside its outline.

1. Click a face of a body.
2. Press Sketch. The rail says it is on a face.
3. Choose Project. The edges of the face are in the sketch.
4. Press Finish Sketch, then click inside the outline to [extrude](doc:extrude) it.

![](image:projected)

The edges come in as ordinary lines, arcs and circles that you can [trim](doc:trim), [delete](doc:sketch-delete) or draw against.

## If it says to start on a face

Project works only while the sketch is on a face. On a plane it says: Project brings in the edges of the face a sketch is drawn on. Start the sketch on a face. Press Escape, pick the face, and press Sketch again.

## Where a part meets the plane

**Intersection**, below Project in the rail, works on any plane: it brings in the outline the parts have where they cross the plane you are drawing on, at whatever angle or offset it stands. A plane that reaches no part says so.

> Start a sketch on a face as in [start a sketch](doc:start-a-sketch).

projected.alt: The top face of a block, projected into a sketch on it

articles.title: Delete in a sketch
articles.summary: Remove one line, arc or circle and leave the rest.
articles.keywords: delete remove erase sketch line primitive clear backspace cut away
articles.body:
1. Click the line, arc or circle. It is picked.
2. Choose Delete in the rail, or press {{key:delete}}.

![](image:picked)

Only that one piece goes. The rest of the sketch stays as it was. A picked point takes the lines and curves that end on it along. Points that nothing uses any more go too, and so do the constraints that named the piece.

Shift-click to pick several first. To take back a delete, press {{key:undo}}.

> To remove a part of a line and not the whole line, use [trim](doc:trim).

picked.alt: A line picked, and Delete in the rail

articles.title: Polygon, slot and point
articles.summary: Draw a regular polygon, a slot with round ends, or a single point.
articles.keywords: polygon hexagon triangle pentagon octagon regular slot oblong rounded slot keyway point dot vertex sketch shape
articles.body:
## Polygon

1. In a sketch, choose Polygon in the rail. It starts as a hexagon; Triangle, Pentagon and Octagon are beside it.
2. Click the centre.
3. Click where one corner goes. The polygon is drawn round a dashed circle through its corners.

Its sides stay equal and its corners stay on that circle, so typing one side's length sizes the whole polygon.

## Slot

1. Choose Slot in the rail.
2. Click the centres of its two round ends.
3. Click beside them to set how wide it is.

The straight sides stay tangent to both ends, and the two ends stay one size.

## Point

Choose Point and click. A point on its own is something to measure from, mirror about or turn a pattern round; it is never part of an area.

articles.title: Spline, ellipse and text
articles.summary: Draw a smooth curve through points, an ellipse, or letters to extrude.
articles.keywords: spline curve smooth bezier freeform organic ellipse oval text letters lettering font engrave emboss label sketch
articles.body:
## Spline

1. Choose Spline in the rail.
2. Click the points the curve should run through, in order.
3. Click the first point again to close it, or press Enter or Escape to end it where it is.

The points are ordinary points: drag them to reshape the curve, snap other lines to them, size the distances between them. A closed spline, or one closed by lines, is an area to extrude, and the solid has exactly the curve you see.

## Ellipse

Ellipse is a variant of Circle in the rail. Click its centre, then the end of one axis (which also sets its turn), then beside that axis for how wide it is.

## Text

1. Choose Text in the rail.
2. Type the text, its height in millimetres from the baseline to the top of a capital, and where its baseline starts.
3. Press Done.

The letters, set in Archivo, become lines and curves like anything you draw: each letter is an area to extrude, raised for embossing or cut away for engraving. Move them afterwards with [Modify, Transform](doc:sketch-modify).

articles.title: Offset, mirror, pattern and transform
articles.summary: Copy what is picked beside itself, mirror it, repeat it, or move, turn and scale it.
articles.keywords: offset parallel copy mirror symmetric reflect pattern array repeat linear polar circular rotate move scale transform sketch modify
articles.body:
Pick the lines, circles or arcs to change (Shift-click for more than one), then choose Modify in the rail. A bar opens at the foot of the canvas; Done keeps the change, Escape or Cancel drops it.

- **Offset**: a copy that stands the given distance off. Joined lines stay joined at their corners. A positive distance goes to the left of a line's direction and outward from a circle or arc.
- **Mirror**: pick what to mirror and last the line to mirror it about. The copy is held symmetric to the original, so it follows when the original changes.
- **Pattern**: Linear repeats along a step in X and Y; Polar turns the copies round the point picked last, or round the sketch's origin without one. Count counts the original.
- **Transform**: moves the picked elements by X and Y, turns them round their middle and scales them.

articles.title: Exact sizes in a sketch
articles.summary: Every line and circle shows its size, and the size can be typed.
articles.keywords: dimension size length diameter radius millimetre exact type value snap grid step units inch edit number smart dimension measure
articles.body:
A sketch is drawn by eye and then made exact. Every size is a number you can click.

1. Draw a line, a rectangle or a circle. Its size is written beside it, in millimetres.
2. Click the number and type another. Press Enter.
3. Escape leaves the number as it was. Clicking away applies what you typed.

![](image:lengths)

The shape follows the number: a rectangle stays a rectangle, a circle keeps its centre. A circle shows its diameter, marked ⌀. A line shows its length. An arc shows its radius, marked R.

## Draw in steps of a size

To make the pointer land on round numbers, turn on the grid snap.

1. Press Quick settings at the bottom right and choose Units & Grid.
2. Turn on **Snap to grid**.
3. Set the **Grid step**, 1 mm to begin with.

![](image:grid)

New points then land on the grid. A click near an existing point still joins it first, so closed shapes stay closed.

## Units

The same panel has Length (mm, cm, m, in, ft) and Numbers (Decimal or Fractions, for inches and feet).

## Sizes from variables

The sizes on a sketch are plain numbers. A number in a step's own panel, such as the Offset of a sketch or the distance of an extrude, can be an expression that uses a variable. See [variables](doc:variables).

> A size you type while drawing, such as a length for a line or both sides of a rectangle, stays as a dimension afterwards. See [line](doc:line) and [rectangle](doc:rectangle).

lengths.alt: A rectangle with its two lengths, each one a field to click

grid.alt: Units & Grid, with Snap to grid on and its Grid step

articles.title: Constraints
articles.summary: Say how lines relate: parallel, perpendicular, horizontal, equal, tangent and more.
articles.keywords: constraint parallel perpendicular horizontal vertical coincident concentric equal tangent angle lock fix relate geometric relation mate symmetric midpoint collinear point on curve reference driven distance
articles.body:
A constraint is a rule about the drawing: these two lines stay parallel, this one stays level. It is how a sketch says what it means, not only where its points are.

1. In a sketch, click a line to pick it. Shift-click to pick a second one.
2. The Constraints bar appears at the bottom of the canvas with the ones that fit what you picked.
3. Click one. A small mark shows on the drawing. Click the mark to take the constraint out again.

![](image:bar)

## What fits what

- **One or more lines**: Horizontal, Vertical, Fix.
- **Two lines**: also Parallel, Perpendicular, Angle and Equal (the same length).
- **Two circles or arcs**: Equal (the same size) and Concentric (the same centre).
- **A line and a circle or arc, or two of them**: Tangent.
- **Two lines**: Collinear, which lays them on one straight, and Ratio, which holds one as a multiple of the other's length. Its mark shows the multiple; click it to type another.
- **Three lines, or two pairs**: Equal angle: the angle from the first to the second stays the one from the second to the third, or the one between the second pair.
- **Any two elements**: Coincident, which brings their nearest ends together.
- **A point and a line**: Point on, Midpoint, and Distance to line. Click right on a line's end to pick the point and not the line.
- **A point and a circle or arc**: Point on.
- **Two points**: Horizontal and Vertical, which level them or stand one above the other, and Distance, Horizontal distance and Vertical distance, each held at what it measures now and written on the drawing to type another.
- **Two points and a line, or three points**: Symmetric, about the line or about the point picked last.
- **A line or circle with a size**: Reference, which keeps its size for reading only. It is shown in brackets and no longer moves the drawing; Reference again makes it drive again.

A button that cannot apply to what you picked is not shown.

## The marks

![](image:marks)

A mark stands beside each constrained line: H for horizontal, V for vertical, ∥ for parallel, ⊥ for perpendicular and so on. A rectangle comes with H and V on its sides already. Click a mark to remove the constraint, and the drawing is free again.

## Angle

Pick two lines and choose Angle. The angle they stand at now is written on the drawing as ∠ and a number in degrees. Click it to type another, between 0 and 180, and press Enter.

## Keys

The keys, in the keymap you use: Parallel {{key:constrain-parallel}}, Perpendicular {{key:constrain-perpendicular}}, Horizontal or vertical, whichever is nearer {{key:constrain-aligned}}, Coincident {{key:constrain-coincident}}, Concentric {{key:constrain-concentric}}, Equal {{key:constrain-equal}}, Tangent {{key:constrain-tangent}}, and Lock, the button called Fix, {{key:constrain-fix}}. Horizontal, Vertical and Angle have no key to begin with; give them one in [Settings, Shortcuts](doc:settings-shortcuts).

## What the sketch says about itself

- The bar at the foot of the canvas counts how much is still free to move, as freedoms left, down to Fully defined.
- Lines, curves and points the constraints hold entirely turn green; blue ones can still move.
- A point drawn on the origin snaps to it and is held there. Without one point held, a sketch can always slide, so it is never fully defined.
- When a change is refused, the marks of the constraints it contradicts turn red, even those that are normally hidden, until the next change is kept.
- A constraint that only restates the others gets a dashed yellow mark. It does no harm, and taking it out keeps the sketch clear.

## What it does

A constraint moves the drawing at once: two lines made parallel turn until they are, and they stay parallel when you drag a point or type a size afterwards. If two constraints cannot both hold, the newer one is refused and the app says which ones disagree.

If the solver cannot be loaded in this window, Bezier says so when it starts: Constraints are kept, not solved yet. They are then stored with the sketch and shown, and take effect the next time the solver is there. Sizes you type move the drawing either way.

If a constraint does not fit what you picked, the bar or the key says why, in words such as Select exactly two lines.

> To round or cut a corner between two lines, see [chamfer or fillet a corner](doc:sketch-corner). To type exact sizes, see [exact sizes](doc:dimensions).

bar.alt: Two lines picked, and the constraints that fit them

marks.alt: Two lines with a Parallel constraint, shown by a mark

articles.title: Chamfer or fillet a corner in a sketch
articles.summary: Cut the corner where two lines meet, or round it.
articles.keywords: corner chamfer fillet round bevel sketch two lines size radius cut corner break edge 2d
articles.body:
Use this on a corner of the drawing itself, before you extrude. To round an edge of a finished body, see [fillet](doc:fillet).

1. Pick the two lines that meet at the corner: click one, Shift-click the other.
2. In the Constraints bar, type a **Corner size** in millimetres. It starts at 2.
3. Choose **Fillet** for an arc that touches both lines, or **Chamfer** for a straight cut across the corner.

![](image:corner)

![](image:done)

- A **fillet** has the size as its radius. The arc touches both lines smoothly.
- A **chamfer** cuts each line back by the size and closes the gap with a straight line.
- Pressing Enter in the size field makes a fillet.

Undo takes it back and leaves the two lines as they were.

## If it says no

- Select the two lines that meet at the corner. The two lines must share their end.
- A 5 mm fillet does not fit on those lines. The size is longer than the lines allow. Type a smaller one.
- Those lines run straight on. There is no corner when two lines are in one line.

Fillet and Chamfer are buttons only while the two lines you picked meet at a corner.

corner.alt: Two lines picked, with Corner size, Fillet and Chamfer in the bar

articles.title: Several shapes, holes and areas
articles.summary: How a sketch with more than one shape is read, and what gets extruded.
articles.keywords: areas hole inside shape island profile several crossing overlap extrude sketch region nested multiple loops pocket
articles.body:
A sketch can hold many shapes. Bezier finds every closed area in it, and you choose which to pull up.

- Two separate shapes in one sketch are two areas, and each is extruded on its own.
- A shape inside another is a hole in it.
- Lines that cross themselves offer each of the areas they enclose.
- A second sketch drawn before the first is extruded leaves both extrudable.

![](image:areas)

## Choose an area

Click the area you want. It is filled, and clicking it offers [Extrude](doc:extrude). Shift-click more areas of the same sketch to extrude them together as one step. Escape takes the offer away.

With nothing clicked, the Extrude command in the rail offers the areas of the newest sketch that have not been used yet.

## When there is no area to click

A shape that is not closed has no area. Its lines may only be close to each other, not joined. Close the gap by drawing to the point, or [trim](doc:trim) the overshoot. Construction lines and [centerlines](doc:centerline) never make an area.

Back to [sketching in five minutes](doc:sketch).

areas.alt: A sketch with a shape inside another, and the outer area clicked

articles.title: Change a sketch afterwards
articles.summary: Open an old sketch, edit it in place, move it off its plane.
articles.keywords: edit reopen sketch history change offset plane move later modify redo parametric roll back update drawing
articles.body:
A finished sketch is not set in stone. Change it and everything built from it is built again.

## Draw in it again

1. Open Items and double-click the sketch. The sketch tools come back, with the drawing as it was.
2. Change what you want: click a number and type another, draw more, [trim](doc:trim) or [delete](doc:sketch-delete) a line.
3. Press Finish Sketch. The part built from it follows.

![](image:editing)

## Move it off its plane

1. Open Items and click the sketch once. Its numbers open on the right.
2. **Offset** sets how far the sketch stands off its plane, in millimetres. The part built from it moves with it.

![](image:offset)

The same panel shows the sketch's Plane, and the face it stands on under On face, if any. Geometry says it is edited by drawing in the sketch.

The Offset can be an expression that uses a variable. See [variables](doc:variables).

> A sketch that has been built from is not drawn in the model any more, and its row in Items is dimmed. Selecting it brings it back. See [items](doc:items).

editing.alt: A sketch reopened from Items, with the sketch tools back in the rail

offset.alt: A sketch selected in Items, with its Offset

articles.title: Finish a sketch and what comes next
articles.summary: Leave the sketch and turn what you drew into a part.
articles.keywords: finish sketch done enter exit leave extrude area click close accept ok end stop escape
articles.body:
1. Press **Finish Sketch**, the top button of the rail, or press Enter.
2. Click inside an area you drew. An arrow and a distance field appear: that is [Extrude](doc:extrude).
3. Type a distance and press Enter. Or press Escape: the offer is taken back and nothing was built.

![](image:button)

The Extrude ⌄ menu beside the field has Direction (Forward, Backward or Symmetric) and Result (New, Add or Cut). If the new part reaches into another body, Bezier asks what to do: Join, Cut from that body, or keep it as a New body. See [extrude](doc:extrude).

## Other ways out

- Press Escape until nothing is left to put down: it cancels a shape you are drawing, puts the tool away, and then leaves the sketch.
- Press Sketch in the rail again.

A sketch with nothing drawn in it is dropped. A sketch with a drawing is kept, as a step in the project. It shows in Items, and you can go back into it. See [change a sketch afterwards](doc:reopen-sketch).

> Several sketches can wait at once. Each keeps its own plane, and every closed area in them can be clicked. See [several shapes, holes and areas](doc:sketch-areas).

button.alt: The Finish Sketch button at the top of the sketch rail

articles.title: Extrude
articles.summary: Pull a closed sketch area, or a face, into a solid, or push it into one to cut.
articles.keywords: extrude pull push pad boss cut height depth solid body distance direction symmetric new add
articles.body:
## From a sketch

1. Draw a closed shape in a [sketch](doc:start-a-sketch) and finish it.
2. Click inside the shape, or choose Extrude under Tools, or press {{key:extrude}}. An arrow and a distance field appear.
3. Drag the arrow or type a distance.
4. Press Enter. The step is added to the history.

![](image:gizmo)

Nothing is built until a distance is given. Escape takes the arrow away again.

## Options

Press **Extrude ⌄** beside the field.

- **Direction**: Forward, Backward or Symmetric about the sketch.
- **Result**: a New body, or added to a body, or cut from one.

![](image:options)

## From a face

Select a face of a body and drag its arrow. A positive distance adds material; a negative one cuts, and the sign is the only choice there is. The part is drawn live as you drag.

> When the new part runs into another, Bezier asks whether to join it, cut it from the other, or keep it apart.

gizmo.alt: The arrow and distance field on a rectangle

articles.title: Fillet and chamfer
articles.summary: Round an edge, or cut it at an angle.
articles.keywords: fillet chamfer round bevel edge radius blend corner smooth cut
articles.body:
1. Click an edge of a body. A handle appears on it.
2. Drag the handle away from the edge for a round, or push it back through the edge for a bevel. Or click the value and type a size, then press Enter.
3. The shape follows while you drag; it is built when you let go.

![](image:handle)

## Fillet or chamfer

The menu beside the value switches the same handle between Fillet and Chamfer. Closing the menu changes nothing.

![](image:menu)

## Change it later

- Click a rounded face to reopen its radius. A radius of zero removes the fillet.
- Click several edges to round them together.

> A fillet keeps the edge it was given when an earlier step changes, such as the height of the body. That is how Bezier names edges; see how history stays right.

handle.alt: The handle on an edge, with its value

menu.alt: The menu that switches between Fillet and Chamfer

articles.title: Shell
articles.summary: Hollow a body out, leaving walls of an even thickness and the faces you chose open.
articles.keywords: shell hollow wall thickness open face hollow out
articles.body:
1. Click the face, or faces, to leave open. Hold Shift for more than one.
2. Choose Shell under Tools, or press {{key:shell}}. The body is hollowed with walls of 2 mm.
3. Open Items, click Shell, and change **Thickness**.

![](image:inspector)

If nothing is selected, Bezier says to select at least one face.

inspector.alt: The Shell step in Items, with its Thickness

articles.title: Hole
articles.summary: Drill a hole into a face: plain, counterbored or countersunk.
articles.keywords: hole drill bore counterbore countersink diameter depth through screw
articles.body:
1. Choose Hole under Tools, then click the face to drill. The hole is made where you click.
2. Open Items, click Hole, and set what it is:

- **Diameter** and **Depth**, or **Through all**.
- **Style**: Simple, Counterbore or Countersink. A counterbore adds a head diameter and depth; a countersink adds an angle.
- **X** and **Y** move it on the face.

![](image:inspector)

Without a face, Bezier says what to click.

## An existing hole

Click the wall of a hole that is already there, for instance in an imported part, and type another radius. It stays editable afterwards.

inspector.alt: The Hole step in Items, with its style and diameter

articles.title: Revolve
articles.summary: Turn a sketch around an axis to make a round part.
articles.keywords: revolve spin lathe turn axis round rotate profile angle bottle
articles.body:
1. Draw a closed shape in a [sketch](doc:start-a-sketch) and finish it.
2. Choose Revolve under Tools, or press {{key:revolve}}. The shape is turned through a full circle.
3. In Items, click Revolve to change the **Axis** (the sketch's own horizontal or vertical), the **Angle**, and the **Result**: a new body, added to one, or cut from one.

![](image:inspector)

Without a closed shape, Bezier says to draw one first.

inspector.alt: The Revolve step in Items, with Axis, Angle and Result

articles.title: Combine: union, subtract, intersect
articles.summary: Join bodies into one, cut one from another, or keep only where they overlap.
articles.keywords: combine boolean union subtract intersect join cut merge bodies overlap difference
articles.body:
1. Pick two bodies: the one to keep first, then Shift-click the other. In Items, click one body row and Cmd-click or Ctrl-click the second.
2. Choose Combine under Tools, or press {{key:union}}. The step starts as a join.
3. In Items, click the step. **Operation** is Join, Cut or Intersect, and **Keep tools** keeps the second body.

The keys for the three: Union {{key:union}}, Subtract {{key:subtract}}, Intersect {{key:intersect}}.

![](image:inspector)

With fewer than two bodies picked, Bezier says: Select two bodies.

inspector.alt: The Combine step in Items, with its Operation

articles.title: Split
articles.summary: Cut a body in two with a plane, or along one of its own faces.
articles.keywords: split cut divide plane two halves lid separate section body
articles.body:
1. Pick the body.
2. Press {{key:split}}. The body is cut in two along the XY plane, and the two halves are bodies of their own.
3. In Items, click Split. Choose the **Plane** (XY, XZ or YZ), the **Offset** from it, and a **Tilt** about X or Y.

![](image:inspector)

## Along a face

Pick the body, then Shift-click the face to split along, and press the key. This takes a lid off a part.

inspector.alt: The Split step, with its plane and offset

articles.title: Move and rotate
articles.summary: Move a body along an axis or turn it about one, by dragging or by typing exact numbers.
articles.keywords: move rotate translate turn position gizmo copy offset pivot arrow axis distance angle
articles.body:
1. Double-click a body to pick all of it, or pick it in Items. Press {{key:move-rotate}}.
2. A gizmo appears on it. Drag an arrow to move along that axis; drag a ring to turn about it. Or click an arrow, and type the distance or angle.
3. **Copy** leaves the original in place and moves a copy.
4. Press Done.

![](image:gizmo)

- The centre handle moves the pivot the rotation turns about, without changing the model.
- Escape while dragging cancels, and nothing is written.
- With several bodies and nothing picked, Bezier asks which one to move.

**One face or one edge.** Click a face or an edge on its own and press {{key:move-rotate}}: only that face or edge moves, and the faces beside it follow. Raising one top edge tilts the top and the sides that meet it. A move that would bend a face, or a curved face next to it, is refused with the reason, and nothing is written. To move the whole body, double-click it.

Each move, copy or turn is a step in the history and can be undone.

gizmo.alt: The move and rotate gizmo on a body

articles.title: Scale
articles.summary: Make a body larger or smaller by a factor.
articles.keywords: scale resize grow shrink factor size enlarge reduce
articles.body:
1. Pick the body.
2. Choose Scale under Transform, or press {{key:scale}}.
3. In Items, click Scale and type a **Factor**: 2 doubles it, 0.5 halves it.

![](image:inspector)

inspector.alt: The Scale step with its Factor

articles.title: Mirror
articles.summary: Add a mirrored copy of a body across a plane.
articles.keywords: mirror reflect symmetric copy flip plane
articles.body:
1. Pick the body.
2. Choose Mirror under Transform. A mirrored body is added beside it.
3. In Items, click Mirror to choose the **Plane** (YZ, XZ or XY), an **Offset**, and whether to **Keep original**.

![](image:inspector)

inspector.alt: The Mirror step and the two bodies it made

articles.title: Align
articles.summary: Set one body against another, face to face.
articles.keywords: align mate place against contact face to face snap position flush
articles.body:
1. Click a flat face of the body to move.
2. Shift-click the flat face of the other body to set it against.
3. Choose Align under Transform. The body turns until its face looks at the other and slides until their middles meet.
4. In Items, click Align for a **Gap** between the faces, or **Same direction** to have both faces look the same way.

The step keeps both faces, so when the other body moves or grows, the aligned one follows.

articles.title: Loft
articles.summary: A solid that runs from one sketched shape to another.
articles.keywords: loft blend transition skin sections round to square taper
articles.body:
1. Draw a closed shape in one sketch, and another in a second sketch on a parallel plane (use the plane's **Offset**), or a leaning one.
2. Choose Loft under Tools. The two latest sketches with one closed shape each are joined; a sketch picked in Items is used first.
3. In Items, click Loft to choose **From sketch** and **To sketch**, **Straight sides** for flat faces between the sections, and the **Result**: a new body, added to one, or cut from it.

articles.title: Sweep
articles.summary: Carry a sketched shape along a path: a pipe, a handle, a rail.
articles.keywords: sweep path pipe tube handle rail along follow
articles.body:
1. Draw the path as lines, arcs or a spline joined end to end, in a sketch of its own. Leave it open, or close it into a loop.
2. Draw the shape to carry in another sketch, standing across the start of the path.
3. Choose Sweep under Tools. The latest closed shape is carried along the latest open path.
4. In Items, click Sweep to change the **Profile sketch**, the **Path sketch** or the **Result**.

A path that branches, or whose pieces do not join, is refused and says so.

articles.title: Wrap
articles.summary: Lay text or a shape round a cylinder, raised from it or cut into it.
articles.keywords: wrap emboss engrave text logo cylinder round label deboss raised
articles.body:
1. Draw the text or shape in a sketch on a plane beside the round face, for example the XZ plane moved out with **Offset**.
2. Pick the round face.
3. Choose Wrap under Tools. The shapes are laid round the face as long as they were drawn, standing 1 mm proud.
4. In Items, click Wrap to set the **Height**: positive raises it, negative cuts it in.

A shape wider than a quarter of the way round is refused; make it smaller or the face larger.

articles.title: Joint
articles.summary: Let one part turn or slide on another, between limits.
articles.keywords: joint hinge revolute slider assembly mate move limits rotate slide
articles.body:
1. Click a face of the part that moves.
2. Shift-click the face it moves on: a round face turns it about its axis, a flat face about the line through its middle, or slides it along that line.
3. Choose Joint under Transform.
4. In Items, click Joint for the **Kind** (revolute to turn, slider to slide), the **Angle** or **Distance**, and the least and most it may go. A value past a limit stops at the limit.

The joint holds on to the face: when the other part moves, the joined one goes with it.

To list the parts and how many of each there are, use Export > **Bill of materials**.

articles.title: Pattern
articles.summary: Repeat a body in a line or around an axis.
articles.keywords: pattern array repeat linear circular copies count step spread
articles.body:
1. Pick the body.
2. Choose Pattern under Transform. Copies are made at once.
3. In Items, click Pattern. Set the **Count**, choose **Linear** or **Circular** as the arrangement, and its **Step** in X, Y and Z, or the **Axis** and the **Spread** in degrees for a circle.

![](image:inspector)

Change the count and the bodies follow.

inspector.alt: The Pattern step with its Count

articles.title: Bodies: name, hide, duplicate, remove
articles.summary: What can be done with a body as a whole.
articles.keywords: body bodies name rename hide show isolate eye duplicate copy remove delete
articles.body:
Bodies are listed at the top of Items.

- **Name** a body: double-click it, type, press Enter.
- **Hide** it with the eye. Alt-click the eye to show only that body, and again to show the rest.
- **Duplicate** the picked body with {{key:duplicate}}: the copy is a body of its own, beside the original.
- **Remove** a body with the delete button of its row, or press {{key:delete}} with the whole body picked.
- **Delete faces** from a body: pick a rounding, a bevel, a boss or a pocket and press {{key:delete}}. The faces around close the gap, so a rounded edge is sharp again. Where they cannot (the top of a box), Bezier says so and leaves the body as it was.

Each of these is a step in the history and can be undone, hiding included.

![](image:list)

list.alt: Two bodies in Items, one named Lid

articles.title: Select faces, edges and bodies
articles.summary: Click, add with Shift, drag a rectangle, and narrow what a click can pick.
articles.keywords: select selection pick click shift multiple filter faces edges bodies rectangle all deselect tab
articles.body:
- **Click** picks exactly what is under the pointer.
- **Shift-click** adds a second one, or takes it off again.
- **Double-click** a body picks all of it and opens Move/Rotate.
- **Drag** on empty space draws a rectangle that selects what it touches; hold Shift to add to the selection.
- **Select all** is {{key:select-all}}. **Deselect** is {{key:deselect}}, or a click on empty space. A click on empty space with Shift held leaves the selection alone.

## The filter

Press {{key:filter-cycle}} to change what a click can pick: Anything, Faces, Edges or Bodies. The current one is named at the bottom, "Selecting Faces · Tab to change". A small hole wall is easier to pick with the filter on Faces.

![](image:filter)

filter.alt: The selection filter named in the corner

articles.title: Wireframe, X-Ray and Shaded
articles.summary: Choose how bodies are drawn: solid, as their edges only, or see-through, and what is drawn around them.
articles.keywords: wireframe xray x-ray zebra curvature analysis smooth continuity shaded display mode edges transparent see through hidden lines grid axes show hide shading render style appearance
articles.body:
Shaded is the usual way to look at a model. Wireframe and X-Ray are for seeing what is behind a face: a hole that runs through, an edge on the far side, a body inside another.

1. Open a project with at least one body.
2. Press Quick settings at the bottom right and choose Display.
3. Under Shading, choose Shaded for solid faces, Wireframe to see only the edges, or X-Ray to see through the faces.

![](image:panel)

![](image:xray)

The choice stays until you change it.

## Checking a surface

Under **Surface analysis**, **Zebra** draws the model as the reflection of a room of light bars: where two faces meet smoothly the stripes run on, where they only touch they kink, and where they meet at an edge they break. **Curvature** colours the surface by how tightly it bends: blue is flat, green gentle, red a radius of about 5 mm or less. **Off** goes back to Shaded.

## What is drawn around the model

Below Shading are two buttons that stay pressed while the thing is shown: **Edges** and **Axes**. Press one to hide it, and again to bring it back. The grid is under Units & Grid, with everything else about it: **Show grid**, **Grid on** for the plane it lies in (XY, YZ or ZX), and Snap to grid.

Under **Look**, marked Every workspace, are the Theme (System, Light or Dark) and Detail while modelling, which is Automatic, Full or Light. Light draws curves coarser on a very large model; exports stay full. These hold everywhere, not only for this model, and are explained under [viewport settings](doc:settings-viewport) and [appearance](doc:settings-appearance).

The three sections are the tabs across the top of the panel: View, Display and Units & Grid. The panel opens on the one you looked at last.

> To look at the model from another side, see [standard views](doc:standard-views). To cut it open instead of seeing through it, see [section view](doc:section-view).

articles.title: Square up to a face
articles.summary: Look straight at a face, centred, without reaching for the orientation cube.
articles.keywords: normal to look at orthogonal face align view space centre center square up perpendicular straight on flat spacebar
articles.body:
Use this to look straight at a face before you sketch on it, measure it or check a hole.

1. Move the pointer over the face you want to look at.
2. Press {{key:view-square}}. The view turns to face it and centres it. On a flat face a sketch starts there too, unless one is open already.

![](image:before)

![](image:after)

On a curved face the view squares up to the surface at the pointer, and no sketch starts.

With the pointer over no face, the same key squares up to the last side picked on the cube, and to Top if none has been picked yet.

## If it turns somewhere else

The pointer has to be over the model, on a face, when you press the key. Over empty space, or over the rails, the key goes to the cube side instead. You can change the key in Settings, Shortcuts. See [shortcuts](doc:settings-shortcuts).

> To go back to a standard side or to the starting view, see [standard views](doc:standard-views). To sketch on the face you are looking at, see [start a sketch](doc:start-a-sketch).

articles.title: Front, top and the other standard views
articles.summary: Jump to one of the six sides, back to the starting view, or fit everything on screen.
articles.keywords: front back top bottom left right view cube orientation reset home fit zoom all isometric default camera side elevation plan zoom extents field of view perspective orthographic
articles.body:
The orientation cube, top right, shows which way you are looking and takes you to any side.

![](image:cube)

1. Click a side of the cube, or press the key for that view.
2. Click an edge of the cube to look along it, halfway between two sides. Click a corner to look from between three.
3. Drag the cube to orbit, the way you would turn a model by hand.
4. When the view is square to an axis, two arrows appear beside the cube. Each turns the view a quarter turn.
5. Press {{key:zoom-fit}} to bring the whole model into view.

The keys: Front {{key:view-front}}, Back {{key:view-back}}, Top {{key:view-top}}, Bottom {{key:view-bottom}}, Right {{key:view-right}}, Left {{key:view-left}}, and back to the starting view {{key:view-reset}}.

## From the View panel

Press Quick settings at the bottom right and choose View. The panel has Zoom to fit, Default, Front, Back, Top, Bottom, Right and Left as buttons. Default is the starting view.

![](image:panel)

Below them:

- **Saved views**: under the standard views, type a name and press **Save view** to keep the camera as it is; click the name to come back to it. They are saved with the project and undo like any edit.
- **Field of view** from Near parallel (5°) to 75°. The view is a true parallel view at every place on the cube (a side, an edge or a corner); turn away from it and the lens is back. With the pointer on the cube, Space goes to the place it is on. A small angle looks like a drawing, a large one like a wide lens; the part stays the same size on screen as you change it.
- **Glide to a chosen view** switches between turning smoothly to the new side and cutting to it.
- Under **Moving the view**, marked Every workspace: **Scrolling with** says whether your scroll comes from a mouse or a trackpad (see [orbit, pan and zoom](doc:navigate)), and **While moving the view** chooses between a sharp and a smooth picture while the view turns.

> Clicking a side of the cube also decides which plane the next sketch is drawn on. See [start a sketch](doc:start-a-sketch).

articles.title: Undo and redo
articles.summary: Step back through what you did, and forward again, including after you reopen the project.
articles.keywords: undo redo step back forward revert history ctrl z cmd z oops mistake reverse
articles.body:
Press {{key:undo}} to take back the last change. Press {{key:redo}} to bring back what you took back. On a keyboard with a Control key, Ctrl and Y redoes as well.

There is no undo button on screen. The keys are the way.

![](image:items)

## What an undo covers

Every change to the project: a step added, a value changed, a body moved, a variable renamed, the project renamed. One action is one undo.

Selections and the camera are not changes, so undo leaves them alone. After an undo the selection is cleared, because the thing it pointed at may be gone.

## While you draw

In a sketch that is still open, {{key:undo}} takes back the last thing you drew, a line or a corner, and not the last step of the project. A shape you are in the middle of is taken back first. When you finish the sketch it becomes one step, and from then on one undo takes back the whole sketch.

> If there is nothing left to take back, Bezier says so: Nothing left to undo, or Nothing to redo.

## After you close the project

Undo still works when you open the project again. The steps are saved beside the project and are taken back only when they still match it exactly. If they do not, you start without an undo, and nothing is undone by mistake.

## What an undo is

An undo is a change like any other. It is written to the project's journal before it is applied, so it survives a crash, and it does not erase the step it reverses from the record. The journal grows a little with every undo.

## What clears redo

Any new change. Once you do something after an undo, the steps you took back are gone, and redo has nothing to bring back.

## Limits

- Bezier keeps the last 100 steps, and fewer when a step is very large, such as an imported file. The oldest give way first.
- Undo waits for a change that is still building. If you press it too early, Bezier says it is still updating the model. Try again in a moment.
- With a sketch that has lines in it and nothing of its own left to take back, Bezier says to finish or clear the sketch first.

See also [variables](doc:variables), which undo like any other change.

items.alt: Items after one undo: the box is back to its sketch, with the extrude taken back

articles.title: Variables and expressions
articles.summary: Name a number once, write a size in terms of it, and change the size everywhere by changing the number.
articles.keywords: variables parameters expression formula equation named values user parameters calculate math units cm inches sin sqrt function
articles.body:
A variable is a name for a number. Write a length or an angle as an expression that uses the name, and the part follows when the number changes.

## Make a variable

1. Press {{key:variables}}. The Variables panel opens. Press it again to close it.
2. Type a name, for example `wall`.
3. Type its value, for example `4 mm`.
4. Press Add, or Enter.

![](image:panel)

A name starts with a letter and uses only letters, digits and `_`. A name cannot be a unit or a function, such as `mm` or `sin`, and two variables cannot share a name. Bezier says why when a name is refused.

To change a variable, edit its name or its value in the list and press Enter. A new name is carried into every expression that uses the old one, in one step. The cross at the end of a row removes the variable.

Beside each variable is what it comes to. A mistake is written there in words instead.

## Use a variable in a step

Open a step in Items, such as an Extrude. A number field, such as a length or an angle, takes an expression as well as a number.

1. Click the field.
2. Type an expression, for example `wall * 3`. A leading `=` is allowed.
3. Press Enter.

The field keeps what you wrote, and the result is shown beside it: `= 12 mm`.

![](image:field)

While you type, a field that cannot be read is marked, and nothing is applied until the expression is whole. A name that does not exist is refused before it reaches the model.

To go back to a plain number, type a number in the field.

Change `wall` in the panel, and only the steps that use it are rebuilt. Undo walks back the variable change and then the expression, one at a time. See [undo and redo](doc:undo-redo).

## Units

A bare number is in millimetres for lengths and degrees for angles. Put a unit after a value to say otherwise:

- Length: `mm`, `cm`, `m`, `in`, `ft`
- Angle: `deg` or `°`, `rad`

`2 cm` is 20. `(a + b) in` works as well. A variable holds the converted number, so `w = 2 cm` shows as 20.

## What an expression can contain

- Numbers, with a point or a comma as the decimal mark: `12.5` or `12,5`.
- Variables, by name.
- `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^` for a power, and brackets. `×` is read as `*`.
- The constant `pi`.
- Functions: `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `sqrt`, `abs`, `round`, `floor`, `ceil`, `min`, `max`.

The trigonometry functions take and give degrees, so `sin(30)` is 0.5. `min` and `max` take several values: `max(wall, 3)`. If you write decimals with a comma, separate the values with a semicolon: `max(1,5; 2)`.

A variable may use another one, in any order. Two that lead back to each other are refused, and the loop is named.

> Expressions are written in the number fields of a step's panel in Items.
