articles.title: Import a file
articles.summary: Bring a STEP part, a scanned mesh, a drawing or a picture into the project by picking the file or dropping it on the window.
articles.keywords: import open file step stp stl obj dxf svg scan mesh drawing picture image photo png jpg jpeg webp tiff heic drop drag insert load bring in upload
articles.body:
## Pick a file

1. Choose File on the left rail. Or press {{key:import}}.
2. Choose the file.

![](image:insert)

## Or drop it

Drag a file from your desktop over the window. The whole window is the target, the rail and the title bar included. A drop area follows the pointer.

![](image:drop)

Let go and the file is imported. Files that can never be read, such as films, PDFs and archives, get no drop area.

## What can come in

| File | What it becomes |
| --- | --- |
| STEP (`.step`, `.stp`) | A step called Import, with the part as a body of its own |
| STL (`.stl`), text or binary | A [reference mesh](doc:reference-mesh) |
| OBJ (`.obj`) | A [reference mesh](doc:reference-mesh) |
| DXF (`.dxf`) | A sketch on the XY plane |
| SVG (`.svg`) | A sketch on the XY plane |
| A picture: PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP, ICO, AVIF, TIFF, HEIC | A [picture](doc:reference-image) on the XY plane to draw and model against |

Any other file is refused, and the notice lists what is accepted. 3MF can be exported but not imported.

A picture is read by the window itself, so the formats are the ones this system can decode. PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP and ICO come in everywhere. AVIF, TIFF and HEIC come in where the system reads them, which the Mac app and Safari do. A format the window cannot read is refused by name, with what to do: save a copy as PNG or JPEG.

![](image:items)

## STEP

A STEP file keeps its real geometry, so it is a solid you can fillet, shell, cut and combine like one you made. The step keeps the text of the file inside the project, so the project does not depend on the original file. A large file takes a while: a bar shows reading and then building, and the model is outlined as it arrives. The model cannot be changed while the file is being read.

A part that arrives below the floor, or tilted, is set down on it.

## Meshes

STL and OBJ are triangles and not solids, so they come in only as something to look at and measure against. A mesh may have up to 400,000 triangles. A bigger one is refused with a note to simplify it first.

## Drawings

A DXF or SVG becomes a sketch on the XY plane, named after the file, and it extrudes like one you drew. See [extrude](doc:extrude).

## If it fails

A notice says so, with the reason: a mesh with no triangles, a damaged STL, an OBJ that points at a point it does not have. The project is left as it was.

Undo takes an import back like any other step. See [undo and redo](doc:undo-redo).

drop.alt: The drop area that follows the pointer when a file is dragged over the window

items.alt: Items after importing a STEP part, a mesh and a drawing

articles.title: Pictures: place, size and crop
articles.summary: Put a photograph, a scanned drawing or a logo on a plane, size it, crop it and move it, to draw and model against.
articles.keywords: picture image photo png jpg jpeg webp gif bmp tiff heic avif canvas underlay trace reference crop resize scale rotate opacity plane move place calibrate background
articles.body:
A picture is for drawing and modelling against: a photograph of a part to trace, a scanned drawing to bring to size, a logo to fit. It is not a solid and not a sketch. It is drawn on a plane, see-through, and a click on the model goes through it to the model.

## Bring one in

Choose File on the left rail, or press {{key:import}}, or drop the picture on the window. See [import](doc:import) for the formats.

It comes in on the XY plane, whole, with its longer side 100 mm, and it is selected: its handles are on the canvas and its numbers are in a panel.

A large picture is brought down to 3072 pixels on its longer side before it is kept, and the project keeps it as one small file, so a photograph from a phone does not make the project heavy. A picture that is small enough is kept exactly as it is.

## Size and place it

In the panel, Size is chosen to begin with.

- **Drag a corner** to scale the picture about the opposite corner, which stays where it is. The proportions are kept. Hold Shift to stretch freely, or untick Keep proportions in the panel.
- **Drag the disc in the middle** to move it along its plane.
- **Drag the small circle above it** to turn it. Hold Shift to turn in steps of 15°.
- **Type the numbers.** Width and Height are the size shown, in millimetres, so a drawing that is 210 mm wide on paper can be set to 210. X and Y are where its middle is on the plane. Turn is the angle. Offset lifts it off the plane along the plane's normal.
- **Plane** puts it on XY, XZ or YZ.
- **Turn 90°** turns it a quarter turn.

Opacity is a slider. A lower value lets the model and the grid show through.

## Crop it

Choose Crop in the panel. The handles on the sides and corners now take part of the picture off instead of scaling it. The picture keeps its scale, so what is left stays where it was, and a dashed outline shows the whole picture. Drag a side outward again to bring back what you took off.

**Reset crop** brings the whole picture back, at the same scale and in the same place.

## Select it again

Click the picture to select it, or choose it in [Items](doc:items). Click anywhere that is not the picture, or press Escape, or close the panel with its cross, to let go of it. The panel can be dragged by its title and snaps to the edges of the window, as the Measure and Section panels do.

## Move it like a part

With the picture selected, press {{key:move-rotate}}. The move arrows appear. Along the plane they change X and Y. Straight out of the plane they change Offset. Copy leaves the picture where it is and makes another one.

## Good to know

- Every change is one step in the history. A drag is one step, and so is a number typed. See [undo and redo](doc:undo-redo).
- The eye in Items hides the picture without deleting it.
- A picture is kept in the project, so the original file is not needed afterwards.

articles.title: Reference mesh
articles.summary: A scan or a bought part, shown as a grey ghost to model against and never part of the solid.
articles.keywords: reference mesh scan stl obj triangles ghost underlay trace fit around measure against canvas
articles.body:
A reference mesh is for modelling around something that already exists: a scan to fit a bracket to, a bought part to leave room for. It is not a solid, so you cannot fillet it or cut with it.

## Bring one in

Import an STL or an OBJ file. See [import a file](doc:import). A notice says As a reference mesh to model against, and a row appears in Items, under History, with the name of the file.

## How it looks

![](image:view)

- Grey and half see-through, so a part inside it still shows.
- Never picked. A click goes through it to the model, so it does not get in the way of selecting anything.
- Not in the bodies list, and not exported. It changes nothing in what you build.

## Where it lands

The mesh keeps the position it has in the file. Its numbers are read as millimetres. It is then moved straight down or up so its lowest point rests on the floor, and it is not moved sideways. If the scan has to line up with your part, model your part around where the scan is.

There is no scale control for it. If the file is in other units, correct it in the program that made it.

## Hide it

Move the pointer over its row in Items and click the eye. The mesh is hidden. Click the eye again to show it. The data stays in the project either way. The bin beside the eye removes the mesh from the project.

![](image:items)

## Size

The mesh is stored inside the project, as text. A detailed scan makes the project bigger and slower to open. The limit is 400,000 triangles; a mesh over it is refused.

view.alt: A grey, see-through mesh standing next to a box

items.alt: The mesh row in Items, with its eye and bin

articles.title: Export
articles.summary: Write the part or a sketch to a file for printing, for another CAD program or for a laser cutter.
articles.keywords: export save step stl 3mf dxf svg print slicer laser cutter cam download file selected body only write out
articles.body:
1. Press **Export**, at the top right.
2. Choose a format.

![](image:menu)

The file is named after the project, with the ending of the format, and goes where your browser saves downloads. In the desktop app a save panel asks where. A notice says when it is done, with the format and the size. Cancelling the panel is fine and writes nothing.

## The formats

- **STEP**: keeps the real geometry. For handing the part to another CAD program.
- **3MF**: a mesh that keeps its units and each body as its own part. For slicers.
- **STL**: a mesh, so curves become triangles. For 3D printing.
- **DXF**: a sketch, exact, in millimetres. For CAM and other CAD programs.
- **SVG**: a sketch as a drawing at true size. For laser cutters.

STEP, 3MF and STL write the part. They say Nothing to export when there is no solid yet.

DXF and SVG write a sketch, the one that is open or the one selected in Items, and are named after it. With no sketch, they are greyed out and the menu says to open or select one.

## Only what is selected

When one or more bodies are selected, the top of the menu offers a box: Only the selected body, or Only the 2 selected bodies. It is ticked. Untick it to export everything.

![](image:selected)

## Close the menu

Press Escape, or click away from it.

> A mesh is a copy of the shape and cannot be edited as a part afterwards. Keep the project for that. Everything you make is saved as you go, so Export is only for sending work out. A [reference mesh](doc:reference-mesh) is not exported.

menu.alt: The Export menu with its five formats

selected.alt: The menu offering to export only the selected body

articles.title: Back to your projects
articles.summary: Leave a project with one click. There is nothing to save first.
articles.keywords: home back projects leave close exit quit library start page save finish
articles.body:
Click the house at the top left of the editor, or press {{key:home}}. The start page opens.

![](image:house)

## Nothing needs saving

Every change is written to disk before it is applied. Leaving does not ask, and a project you come back to is as you left it. See [projects](doc:projects).

## The card

On the way out Bezier takes a picture of the model from the default view, framed on the model, and puts it on the project's card. It is the picture you see on the start page. If the picture cannot be taken, you still leave, and the card keeps the one it had.

## Special cases

- A project you made and did nothing in is not kept. It is removed when you leave, so there is no empty Untitled waiting on the start page.
- A sketch you are in the middle of is finished first, as it is when you leave sketch mode, and then you leave. It is not lost.
- A file still opening is given up when you press the house.
- In a lesson, the house leaves through the lesson. See [Learn](doc:learn).
- Escape does not leave the project. It puts away the tool, the selection or the sketch.

house.alt: The house button at the top left of the editor

articles.title: Simulation: test a part under load
articles.summary: Hold the part, push on it, solve, and read where it is stressed and how far it bends. A worked example with an angle bracket.
articles.keywords: simulation simulate study fea fem finite element analysis stress strain static load test solve von mises safety factor strength deflection bracket fixed support force will it break how strong
articles.body:
Simulation is a [workspace](doc:workspaces) over the model you built in Modeling. A **study** is one test of it: which faces are held, which are loaded, what the part is made of, and how fine the calculation is. The answer is drawn on the part as colour. Simulation never changes the model.

You need a solid body to test. If the part is not closed, the solve says so.

## A worked example: an angle bracket

The part is a flat angle bracket, an L of two arms, 20 mm thick. The end of the short arm is bolted to a wall. The long arm carries 200 N. Two questions: where is the bracket stressed most, and does it hold?

To follow along, draw an L with the [line](doc:line) tool in a sketch and [extrude](doc:extrude) it 20 mm. Any solid works the same way.

### 1. Open Simulation

Choose **Simulation** in the workspace menu at the top left, or press Alt+⌘+2 (Alt+Ctrl+2 on Windows and Linux). A bar of settings appears at the top, with a short list of steps under it.

![](image:bar)

The bar says "Needs support · load". The list ticks each step off as you do it.

### 2. Hold the bracket

1. Choose **Fixed** in the rail. A hint says "Click the faces that are held in place."
2. Click the end face of the short arm. It turns blue and a panel opens: "1 face".
3. Press **Done**.

![](image:fixed)

Fixed means the face cannot move at all, as if it were welded to a wall. See [supports](doc:simulation-supports) for the other two.

### 3. Load the bracket

1. Choose **Force** in the rail and click the top face. The top of an extruded L is one face, so the whole top is chosen.
2. In the panel, select the **Magnitude** field, type `200` and press Enter.
3. Look at **Direction**. The force starts out pushing straight into the face you clicked, which here is −Z, down. That is what we want.
4. Press **Done**, then Esc to put the tool down.

![](image:force)

A force is a total. Spread over the whole top, 200 N is shared by area, so most of it lands on the long arm. See [loads](doc:simulation-loads).

### 4. Solve

Press **Solve** in the bar, or Ctrl+Enter (⌘↩ on a Mac). The button shows its progress and turns into **Cancel**. The solve runs in the background, so you can keep turning the part. The [study browser](doc:simulation-browser) says afterwards how long it took.

### 5. Read the result

![](image:solved)

The part is coloured by von Mises stress, a single number for how hard the material is working at a point. Blue is little, red is most. The legend at the lower right gives the headline numbers. In the picture:

- **Max stress** is 4.01 MPa. The part is green around the foot and the inner corner, where the arms are bent most, and blue towards the free tip, which carries little. The red end of the scale does not show from this side. The peak is on a face turned away from you, or on a very small area, so turn the part to look for it.
- **Max displacement** is 0.308 mm, at the free end of the long arm. The part is drawn bent more than it really is, so you can see it. See [reading the results](doc:simulation-results).
- **Min safety factor** is 12.46. It is the yield strength of the material, 50 MPa for PLA, divided by the stress. Above 2 is comfortable. Below 1 the material would give way. So this bracket is far from failing, and it could be lighter.

Move the pointer over the part to read the stress at any spot. Choose **Displacement** or **Safety factor** in the bar along the bottom to see the others.

Your numbers will differ if your bracket is not the same size. The pattern will not: most stress near the foot and the corner, least at the tip.

### 6. Try a change

- Swap the material in the bar to **Aluminium 6061-T6** and press Solve again. The displacement falls, because aluminium is much stiffer than PLA.
- Go back to Modeling, round the inner corner with a [fillet](doc:fillet), return and Solve. A rounded corner usually carries a lower peak. A small fillet may not show on the default mesh, so try **Fine**.
- Change the study type to **Shape Optimisation** to see what material the loads do not need. See [shape optimisation](doc:simulation-optimisation).

## The bar

From the left:

- **Study type**: the kind of calculation. Two are built: **Static Stress** and **Shape Optimisation**. The others in the list are greyed and marked "soon": Modal Frequencies, Thermal, Thermal Stress, Structural Buckling, Nonlinear Static, Event Simulation, Fatigue and Flow Preview. They cannot be chosen yet.
- **Material** and **Mesh density**: see [material and mesh](doc:simulation-material).
- **Solve**. If a support or a load is missing, the bar says "Needs support", "Needs load" or both. Pressing Solve anyway lists what is missing and does nothing else.

The **Study** button at the top of the rail opens the [study browser](doc:simulation-browser), the list of everything in the study.

## When something changes

A result describes the shape it was solved on. If you change the model, or change the study (a support, a load, the material, the mesh), the colours come off the part and a **Model changed** note appears. Your supports, loads, material and mesh stay. Press Solve again.

Switching back to Modeling puts the part back to its normal look.

The study is kept with the project, on this device. It is not part of the undo history, and a copy or export of the project does not carry it.

## If it does not solve

| The message | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Not ready to solve yet | A support or a load is missing. The message says which. |
| The solve did not settle. Part of the model is free to move. | Add a support, or hold more directions, so every piece is held. |
| The part could not be meshed. It may not be a closed solid. | Fix the model in Modeling first. |
| There is no solid to analyse yet. | Build a body first. |

> The numbers come from a voxel approximation of the part. They show where it is stressed and roughly how much. Check a critical part with a finer mesh before you trust a value.

fixed.alt: The Fixed panel open, with the end of the short arm selected in blue

force.alt: The Force panel with 200 N, the direction pointing down, and the arrow on the top face

solved.alt: The solved bracket coloured by stress, green near the foot and blue at the tip, with the legend at the lower right

articles.title: Supports: hold the part in place
articles.summary: Fixed, Pin and Frictionless stop faces of the part from moving.
articles.keywords: support constraint fixed pin frictionless boundary condition hold clamp anchor restraint bolt slide fixture fixed geometry roller symmetry
articles.body:
A study needs at least one support, or the part would simply fly away. The three supports are in the rail, in the first group of tools.

| Support | What it does | Think of |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Fixed** | The faces cannot move in any direction. | A face bolted or welded to a wall. |
| **Pin** | Only the directions you choose are held: X, Y or Z. | A peg through a hole. |
| **Frictionless** | The faces are held along their normal and free to slide along themselves. | A face resting on a smooth table. |

## Place one

1. Choose the support in the rail. A hint at the top says what to click, for Fixed "Click the faces that are held in place."
2. Click a face of the part. It is added and its panel opens.
3. Click more faces if the same support holds several. Click a face again to take it off. The panel counts them.
4. Press **Done**, or Enter, to close the panel. The tool stays in hand, so the next click on a face starts another support. Press Esc to put the tool down.

![](image:panel)

A round marker on the face shows each support where it sits.

## Pin

A pin has one more choice. In the panel, under **Held directions**, switch **X**, **Y** and **Z** on or off. All three start on. The directions are the model's own axes, not the face's.

![](image:pin)

In the picture Z is off, so the face is held sideways and free to move up and down.

## Change or remove one

Open the [study browser](doc:simulation-browser) and click the row. The panel opens again. **Delete** at the foot of the panel removes the support, and so does the bin at the end of the row.

## Choosing supports well

- Hold what is really held. A bracket bolted down is Fixed on the faces the bolts clamp, not on every face it touches.
- Too few supports leaves part of the model free, and the solve can stop with "The solve did not settle". One Frictionless face alone is not enough: the part can still slide.
- A small face held hard makes a stress peak at its edge. That value is the least reliable in the result.

Next: [loads](doc:simulation-loads). The whole walk-through is in [Simulation](doc:simulation).

articles.title: Loads: force, pressure and gravity
articles.summary: Push on faces with a force or a pressure, or switch gravity on.
articles.keywords: load force pressure gravity weight newton mpa bar direction flip push apply stress boundary self weight
articles.body:
A study needs at least one load. There are three, in the second group of tools in the rail.

## Force

1. Choose **Force** and click the faces it acts on.
2. In the panel select **Magnitude** and type the force in newtons. The default is 100 N. About 10 N is the weight of one kilogram.
3. Choose a **Direction**: −X, +X, −Y, +Y, −Z or +Z. **Flip direction** reverses the one you have.
4. Press **Done**.

The direction starts out pushing straight into the face you clicked. On a face that is not square to an axis none of the six buttons is lit, and the arrow still points into the face until you choose one.

![](image:force)

The force is the total. With several faces it is shared between them by their area. An arrow on the part shows the direction and the size.

## Pressure

Choose **Pressure**, click the faces, and type the pressure in megapascals. A positive pressure pushes into the part. 0.1 MPa is one bar. Pressure always acts across the face, so it has no direction to choose. The default is 0.1 MPa.

![](image:pressure)

Use pressure for something spread evenly over a face, like air or a liquid against a lid. Use force for a weight or a push at a place.

## Gravity

**Gravity** in the rail is a switch, not a tool. It reads **On** or **Off** under its name. On, it adds the part's own weight, 9.81 m/s² downward along −Z. It counts as a load, so a study with only gravity and a support can be solved.

![](image:gravity)

## Change or remove one

Open the [study browser](doc:simulation-browser) and click the row of the load. **Delete** in its panel removes it. Switching Gravity off removes it too.

Next: [material and mesh](doc:simulation-material), then Solve. The whole walk-through is in [Simulation](doc:simulation).

articles.title: Material and mesh density of a study
articles.summary: Choose what the part is made of and how fine the calculation is.
articles.keywords: material pla petg abs nylon aluminium aluminum steel titanium stainless mesh density resolution coarse medium fine ultra elements yield accuracy speed
articles.body:
Both are chosen in the study bar. They belong to the study, not to the model.

![](image:bar)

## Material

The material sets stiffness, weight and the strength the safety factor is measured against. Stiffer material bends less. Stronger material takes more stress before it gives way. There are eight.

- **Printed polymers**: PLA (printed), PETG (printed), ABS (printed) and Nylon PA12.
- **Metals**: Aluminium 6061-T6, Steel S235, Stainless 304 and Titanium Ti-6Al-4V.

The [study browser](doc:simulation-browser) shows the chosen material's stiffness (E) and yield strength (σy).

> The printed polymers use the strength along the printed layers. Across the layers a printed part is 30 to 50 percent weaker.

## Mesh density

The calculation divides the part into small cells. More cells give a better answer and take longer.

| Choice | About |
| --- | --- |
| Coarse | 6k cells |
| Medium | 24k cells (the default) |
| Fine | 70k cells |
| Ultra | 160k cells |

After a solve the browser shows the real count and the size of one cell in millimetres. If a stress peak sits on one cell, choose a finer mesh and solve again. A value that changes a lot between meshes is not settled yet.

Changing either one takes the colours off the part. Press Solve again. See [Simulation](doc:simulation) for the whole walk-through, and [reading the results](doc:simulation-results) for what comes out.

bar.alt: The material and mesh density choices in the study bar

articles.title: The study browser
articles.summary: A list of the study: its material, supports, loads, mesh and result.
articles.keywords: study browser list supports loads edit delete tree panel summary overview
articles.body:
The browser is the list of everything in the study. Use it to check what is set, to reopen a support or a load, and to delete one.

1. Press **Study** at the top of the rail. The browser opens on the left.
2. Press it again, or the **×** in the browser, to close it.

The browser stays shut until you ask for it, so it never covers the faces you are clicking.

![](image:browser)

It has a section for each part of the study:

- **Material**: the name, stiffness and yield strength.
- **Supports** and **Loads**: one row for each, with its size and the number of faces. Click a row to open its panel and change it. The bin at the end of a row deletes it.
- **Mesh**: the number of cells, or the number it will aim for before a solve.
- **Results**: appears after a solve. It says **Solved** or **Out of date**, the time it took and the number of iterations.

The Modeling [Items](doc:items) panel is not shown in Simulation. Going back to Modeling brings it back.

See [supports](doc:simulation-supports) and [loads](doc:simulation-loads) for what each row opens.

articles.title: Reading the results of a study
articles.summary: Stress, displacement and safety factor drawn on the part, with a scale and a hover readout.
articles.keywords: results stress von mises displacement deformation safety factor legend colour scale contours animate hover max yield fail read interpret
articles.body:
After a solve the part is coloured and two things appear: a **legend** at the lower right and a **results bar** along the bottom.

![](image:legend)

## What is shown

Choose in the results bar:

- **Stress**: von Mises stress in MPa. Red is where the material is working hardest. Compare the peak with the material's yield strength.
- **Displacement**: how far each point moved, in millimetres. It tells you how much the part bends.
- **Safety factor**: yield strength divided by stress. Below 1 the material would yield; below 2 deserves a look. The scale tops out at 8 and the summary at 15.

The legend lists the three headline numbers: **Max stress**, **Max displacement** and **Min safety factor**. The safety factor is coloured as a warning when it falls under 2 and as a failure under 1.

## Read a value

Move the pointer over the part. A marker slides along the legend to the value under the pointer, and a readout in the legend gives the number. Off the part, and while a mouse button is down, the readout says "Hover the model".

![](image:hover)

## How it looks

![](image:bar)

- **Undeformed**, **Actual** or **Exaggerated**: how the part is bent. Exaggerated, the default, scales the largest movement to about six percent of the part's size so you can see it. Actual draws the true movement, which is usually too small to see.
- **Animate**: swings the part between rest and bent. It needs Actual or Exaggerated.
- **Smooth** or **Contours**: a continuous blend, or ten steps of colour. Contours is the default.
- **Hide** or **Show**: takes the colours off the part and brings them back. **Results** in the rail does the same, and reads None before a solve, then Shown, Hidden or Out of date.

## What to do with it

- Red where you did not expect it: check that the support and the load are on the faces you meant.
- A safety factor under 2: thicken the part, add a [fillet](doc:fillet) where the red is, or choose a stronger material, then solve again.
- A peak on a single cell: choose a finer [mesh](doc:simulation-material) and see if it holds.

> The legend notes that the result is a voxel approximation and how many cells it used.

articles.title: Shape optimisation: remove material the loads do not need
articles.summary: Keep a share of the material where the loads need it and show what can go.
articles.keywords: optimisation optimization topology shape simp lightweight lighten remove material keep density generative weight save material
articles.body:
Shape Optimisation is the second study type that is built. It uses the same supports and loads as a static study, then looks for the part of the material that carries them and shows what is left over.

1. Set up [supports](doc:simulation-supports) and [loads](doc:simulation-loads) as usual.
2. In the bar, choose **Shape Optimisation** as the study type. The mesh switches to Coarse, because the calculation solves about forty times.
3. Use the **Keep** slider to choose how much of the material to keep, from 10 to 80 percent. It starts at 35 percent.
4. Press **Solve**. The part updates as the calculation goes.

![](image:bar)

The result is drawn as a density, from 0 to 1, on the legend's scale. The legend gives **Material kept** as a percentage. The results bar shows **Optimised shape** and has no stress, displacement or deformation choices. Material the loads hardly use is left out of the picture.

![](image:result)

> The result is a guide. It does not change your model: no feature is added and nothing is cut. Use it to decide where to put a [hole](doc:hole) or a pocket yourself in Modeling.

articles.title: Drawings: technical sheets of your model
articles.summary: Turn the model into a dimensioned technical drawing: front, top, right and isometric views on a sheet, ready to print or send to a machinist.
articles.keywords: drawings drawing sheet technical 2d blueprint views orthographic projection print paper a4 a3 a2 layout drafting plan engineering drawing paper space dimension title block pdf dxf
articles.body:
Drawings is a [workspace](doc:workspaces) that turns the model into sheets of paper. The views are projected from the real solid, hidden edges included, so they always match it.

![](image:workspace)

Open it from the workspace menu at the top left of the window, the button that names the workspace you are in. Nothing you do here changes the model.

## What is on screen

- **The desk**: the sheet sits on a dark desk. Scroll to pan, or drag the empty desk. Pinch, or hold Ctrl (⌘ on a Mac) and scroll, to zoom about the pointer.
- **The toolbar** along the top: **Dimension**, **Section** and **Detail**, then the zoom controls, then **+ Sheet**, **Update from model** (the circular arrow) and **Export Sheet**. When the window is narrow, or the Items panel is open, the words are left out and only the icons show. Point at one to read its name.
- **The inspector** on the right: an overview of all the sheets, then the groups **Sheet**, **Views**, **Annotations**, **Title Block** and **Branding**. Drag its left edge to make it wider; double-click the edge to reset it.
- **Items** at the left, behind the **Items** button in the rail: the sheets, and what each one shows. See [sheets](doc:drawings-sheets).
- **The status line** at the foot says the size, scale, projection and unit of the active sheet.

## The first sheet

A new project has one sheet, **Sheet 1**, on A3 in first-angle projection. It shows four views: **Front**, **Top**, **Right** and **Isometric**. The scale is chosen for you so that every view fits.

The sheet draws every body that is visible in the model. Hide a body in [Items](doc:items) and it leaves the sheet. A model with no solid shows "No views on this sheet".

## Make a drawing in four steps

1. Build the part in Modeling.
2. Open Drawings and look over the four views. Set the paper in [Sheet size, scale and extra views](doc:drawings-views) if the default does not suit.
3. [Dimension](doc:drawings-dimensions) the lengths that matter, and add tolerance frames if you need them.
4. Fill in the [title block](doc:drawings-title-block) and [export](doc:drawings-export) a PDF or DXF.

## Zoom

The buttons beside the percentage zoom out and in. Press the percentage to fit all the sheets on the desk. Click the desk once, then **F** fits, **+** zooms in and **−** zooms out.

## When the model changes

The views follow the model when its shape changes. If a sheet does not seem to, press **Update from model** and it is projected again.

> Everything you set on a sheet, its dimensions, titles and logo, is saved with the project. A dimension is drawn on paper, not on the model, so changing the model does not move it. Check your dimensions after you change the part.

## Next

- [Sheets and what they show](doc:drawings-sheets)
- [Sheet size, scale and extra views](doc:drawings-views)
- [Dimensions and tolerances](doc:drawings-dimensions)
- [The title block](doc:drawings-title-block)
- [Export as PDF or DXF](doc:drawings-export)

articles.title: Drawing sheets and what each one shows
articles.summary: Add sheets, choose which bodies and sketches each one draws, move between them and delete them.
articles.keywords: sheet sheets add new delete items bodies sketches include overview multiple pages select pan fit second sheet detail drawing set
articles.body:
A drawing can have several sheets, for example one for the part and one for a detail. Each sheet has its own size, views, dimensions and title block.

## Add a sheet

Press **+ Sheet** in the toolbar, or **+** at the top of the Items panel. The new sheet is named **Sheet 2**, **Sheet 3** and so on, and Items opens so that you can choose what it shows.

The new sheet starts with no bodies, so it is blank and **Export Sheet** is greyed out until you tick something. It copies the size, projection, title, author, company, watermark and logo of the sheet you were on. Only the drawing number is new: DWG-002, DWG-003 and so on.

## Choose what a sheet shows

1. Press **Items** in the rail at the left of the Drawings workspace. The panel opens.
2. Under **Included on** the active sheet, tick the **Bodies** you want drawn. **All bodies** ticks them all; **None** clears them.
3. Tick **Sketches** to draw a sketch's lines on every view too. Construction lines are left out.

![](image:items)

A sheet that you have not changed from the start shows every visible body. Once you tick or clear a box, the sheet keeps exactly the list you chose, even when you add bodies later.

Changing what a sheet includes clears its dimensions, because they would no longer point at the same lines.

## Move between sheets

Click a sheet in the list, or click its paper or its name above it on the desk. Only one sheet is active, the one you can edit. The others are drawn as pictures and you cannot click into them.

The **Overview** at the top of the inspector shows all the sheets small. Click or drag in it to move the desk, and press **Fit all** to see them all at once.

## Delete a sheet

Press the bin at the end of its row in Items. The bin is greyed out on the last sheet, which cannot be deleted.

Each row says the size, the drawing number, and how many bodies and sketches the sheet shows.

> Sheets are named by their position, and cannot be renamed. The drawing number in the [title block](doc:drawings-title-block) is what identifies a sheet on paper.

## Related

articles.title: Sheet size, scale and extra views
articles.summary: Choose paper size, projection and scale, show hidden lines, and add a section or detail view.
articles.keywords: sheet size a4 a3 a2 scale projection first angle third angle hidden lines dashed line weight section detail view cut hatch zoom magnify cross section 1:1 2:1
articles.body:
These settings are in the inspector, in the **Sheet** and **Views** groups. They apply to the active sheet only.

![](image:inspector)

## Sheet

- **Size**: A4, A3 or A2, always landscape.
- **Projection**: **First angle** or **Third angle**. It decides where the views sit, and the symbol in the title block says which one the sheet uses. First angle is common in Europe and Asia, third angle in North America.
- **Scale**: **Auto**, or a fixed scale from 1 : 50 to 10 : 1. Auto picks the largest standard scale at which every view fits, and its name shows the scale it chose, for example **Auto (2 : 1)**. Choose a fixed scale to override it.

## Views

- **Hidden lines**: draws the edges behind the part as dashed lines. Switch it off for a cleaner sheet.
- **Line weight**: 0.25, 0.35, 0.5 or 0.7 mm for the visible outline. Hidden lines are drawn thinner.

## Section A–A

Switch on **Section A–A**, or press **Section** in the toolbar. A cut through the part is added to the sheet with the cut face hatched. **Cut height** sets where the cut is, from 5 to 95 percent of the height. It starts at the middle.

Use a section to show what is inside: a hole, a pocket, a wall thickness. Press **Section** again to remove it.

## Detail B

Switch on **Detail B · 2 : 1**, or press **Detail** in the toolbar. A circle is placed on the top view and the part inside it is drawn again, twice as large, as its own view. The **X**, **Y** and **R** fields give the circle's centre and radius in millimetres. Change them to move the detail to the feature you want to show.

## With more views

With more than four views, for example a section and a detail, the sheet lays them out in a grid of six and picks a smaller scale if it must.

> Changing the size, projection, scale, section or detail clears the dimensions on the sheet, because they are measured on the paper. Set these first and dimension afterwards.

## Related

- [Dimensions and tolerances](doc:drawings-dimensions)
- [Drawing sheets](doc:drawings-sheets)

articles.title: Dimensions and geometric tolerances on a sheet
articles.summary: Measure between two points of a view, edit and place the number, and add geometric tolerance frames.
articles.keywords: dimension dimensions measure length tolerance gdt gd&t datum frame feature control flatness position profile parallelism perpendicularity roundness annotation aligned horizontal vertical
articles.body:
A dimension on a sheet is a measured length between two points of one view, drawn with arrows and a number. It is the number a machinist reads, so the sheet needs only the ones that matter.

## Add a dimension

1. Press **Dimension** in the toolbar, or click the desk and press **D**. Small blue dots show where a dimension can start and end.
2. Choose **Aligned**, **Horizontal** or **Vertical** in the line that appears at the foot of the screen. In the isometric view only Aligned is available, and it reads the true length in 3D.
3. Click one end. A larger dot marks it, and the line says "Choose another endpoint in this view".
4. Click the other end, in the same view. The dimension is drawn with the measured length in millimetres.

![](image:tool)

Keep clicking pairs of points to add more. When you are done, press **Esc** to leave the tool, or press **Dimension** again. If you clicked the wrong first point, press **Esc** once to drop it, and **Esc** again to leave the tool.

![](image:made)

Only the ends of visible lines can be picked, and a click that is not near a blue dot does nothing. The same two points are not dimensioned twice.

## Place and edit it

- **Drag** the number to move the dimension line and the text.
- **Double-click** the number to type your own text, for example 40 ±0.1. Press Enter to keep it, or Esc to cancel. The text is only a label; it does not change what is measured.
- To remove one, Tab to its grip until it is focused and press Delete. The grip is named "Move dimension 1", "Move dimension 2" and so on. With the grip focused, the arrow keys nudge it by 1 mm and Shift with an arrow by 5 mm.

The **Annotations** group in the inspector counts the dimensions. **Undo** removes the last one; **Clear** removes them all.

## Geometric tolerances

The same group builds feature control frames, the boxes that say how exact a feature must be.

1. Choose a characteristic: **Position**, **Flatness**, **Perpendicularity**, **Parallelism**, **Roundness** or **Profile**.
2. Type the **Tolerance** in millimetres. It takes digits and a decimal point.
3. Type the **Datum** letter or letters, up to three. Flatness and roundness have no datum, so the field is greyed.
4. Press **Add**.

![](image:frame)

The frames stack upwards from the lower left corner of the sheet, up to six. The **×** beside a frame in the list removes it. The datum letters are text inside the frame: Bezier does not draw a datum symbol on a view.

## Things to know

- Dimensions are drawn on the paper, so they are cleared when something changes the views: size, projection, scale, a section or detail, or the bodies a sheet includes. Dimension last.
- If a dimension reads a number you did not expect, check the scale in the status line: the number is the real length of the part, not the length on the paper.

> Dimensions and frames are drawn as lines and text, so they go into the [PDF and DXF](doc:drawings-export) exactly as you see them.

## Related

- [The title block](doc:drawings-title-block)

articles.title: The title block, watermark and logo
articles.summary: Fill in who made the drawing, its number and revision, and brand the sheet.
articles.keywords: title block drawn by author company drawing number revision date watermark logo svg brand header cartouche stamp draft confidential
articles.body:
Every sheet has a title block in its lower right corner, in the layout of ISO drawings.

## Fill it in

Two ways, which edit the same fields:

- In the inspector, open **Title Block** and fill in **Title**, **Drawing No.**, **Revision**, **Drawn by** and **Company**.
- On the sheet, double-click a field of the block, type, and press Enter. Esc cancels. With the keyboard, Tab to a field and press Enter to edit it.

![](image:block)

The sheet fills in the rest: **Scale**, the **Sheet** number out of the total, today's **Date**, the **Format** and unit, and the projection symbol with its name. You cannot edit these.

A new project's first sheet takes the project's name as its title and a number such as DWG-001. The revision starts as A and the company as Bezier. An empty title is shown as "Untitled".

## Branding

Open **Branding** in the inspector. It starts folded.

- **Watermark**: type a word, for example PROTOTYPE, and it is drawn large and faint across the sheet. **Watermark opacity** appears, from 2 to 30 percent. Clear the field to remove it.
- **Logo**: press **Import…** and choose an SVG file. It takes the place of the company name in the title block. **Replace…** and **Remove** change or take it away.

![](image:branding)

> The logo has to be vector paths with a viewBox, and under 1 MB. Rectangles, circles, text, groups with a transform and links are refused with a message, such as "Convert logo shapes and text to paths". Convert them to paths in your vector program first.

The block, watermark and logo are all part of the [export](doc:drawings-export). A sheet you add later starts with a copy of these settings, see [sheets](doc:drawings-sheets).

articles.title: Export a sheet as PDF or DXF
articles.summary: Save the active sheet as a vector PDF for print or a DXF for CAD and CAM.
articles.keywords: export pdf dxf print save vector cad cam autocad download drawing sheet r2013 millimetres machinist send
articles.body:
1. Make the sheet you want active.
2. Press **Export Sheet** in the toolbar.
3. Choose a format.

![](image:menu)

| Format | For | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **PDF** | Print and review | Vector, at the size of the sheet, in landscape. No picture of the screen is put in it. |
| **DXF** | CAD and CAM | R2013, in millimetres. Visible and hidden lines are on separate layers (VISIBLE and HIDDEN), and the text is kept as text on a layer named ANNOTATIONS. |

The file is named after the drawing number, for example DWG-001.pdf. In a browser it goes to your downloads folder. In the desktop app a save dialog asks where.

Export Sheet is greyed out when the sheet has no views.

Only the active sheet is exported. To export another, choose it and export again.

What you see is what is saved: views, dimensions, tolerance frames, title block, watermark and logo. The blue dimension dots and anything else that only helps while you work are left out.

## If something looks wrong

- Check the sheet before you export. Dimensions that were cleared by a change are not in the file.
- For print, choose the same paper size in the print dialog as the sheet: A3 for an A3 sheet, and print at 100 percent.

articles.title: Visualize: materials, light and renders
articles.summary: Finish the model with materials and studio light, then save a picture or a turntable video of it.
articles.keywords: visualize visualise render rendering presentation pbr materials lighting studio photo realistic appearance look image keyshot product shot colour color finish
articles.body:
Visualize is a [workspace](doc:workspaces) for showing the part, not for changing it. Nothing you do here alters the geometry.

![](image:workspace)

Open it from the workspace menu at the top left of the window. With no solid in the model the window says "Nothing to render yet": build a body in Modeling first. The first time you open Visualize it starts its renderer, which can take a few seconds, and a "Starting the renderer…" note shows meanwhile.

## What is on screen

- **The render** fills the window. It has its own camera, so framing a shot never moves the view you model in. Drag to turn the part and scroll to zoom.
- **The look panel** on the right has three tabs: **Material**, **Environment** and **Camera**. Drag its left edge to make it wider; double-click the edge to reset it.
- **The render bar** at the top: **Turntable**, **Record 360°**, **Frame** and **Capture**.
- **Items** in the rail at the left lists the bodies, as in Modeling.

## Make a first picture

1. In the **Material** tab, pick a material from the library. See [Materials](doc:visualize-materials).
2. In **Environment**, choose a studio. See [Environment and light](doc:visualize-environment).
3. Turn the part with the mouse until you like the view, then press **Frame** if you lose it.
4. Press **Capture**. See [Capture, turntable and video](doc:visualize-render).

## Which bodies a change applies to

Double-click a body in the render, or click it in Items, to pick it. Shift adds more. A single click picks the face under the pointer instead: see [Materials for single faces](doc:visualize-faces). The Material tab says **Apply to:** and names what is picked. With nothing picked, a material goes to all visible bodies.

Each body keeps its own finish.

## Where to go next

- [Materials](doc:visualize-materials)

- [Lights and glowing materials](doc:visualize-lights)
- [Environment and light](doc:visualize-environment)

articles.title: Materials in Visualize
articles.summary: Pick a finish from the library, tint it, and adjust how shiny, metallic or grainy it is.
articles.keywords: material library plastic abs pla metal aluminium steel brass copper wood stone marble ceramic glass rubber leather textile roughness metallic clear coat transmission grain colour tint search drag shiny matte finish appearance
articles.body:
Open the **Material** tab of the look panel. The panel is long: from the top it has the search field, **Apply to:**, **In Use**, **Decal**, and then the library. Scroll down to reach the library.

## Choose a material

1. Pick the body or bodies you want to change, or none for all of them.
2. Press **Done** in **In Use** to fold its controls away. The library moves up.
3. Look in the library. It is grouped by **Plastic**, **Metal**, **Wood**, **Stone**, **Ceramic**, **Glass**, **Rubber**, **Leather**, **Textile** and **Light**. Each tile shows a ball in that finish.
4. Click a tile. It is applied at once.
5. Or drag a tile onto a body in the render to give it that material alone.

The search field at the top, **Search Materials**, filters by name, finish, group or source. "No material matches" shows when nothing fits.

![](image:library)

Some materials are photographed from real surfaces, and the panel says where they come from, for example Poly Haven or GPUOpen. Their maps load when you choose the material, and **Loading maps…** shows while they do.

## In Use and Adjust

**In Use** shows the current material and its controls. Press **Done** to fold the controls away, and **Adjust** to open them again.

![](image:adjust)

- **Tint**: for materials that can be tinted, a colour field, a hue bar, a row of suggested colours, and a hex field. Type a code such as #416FAB, or click a suggested colour.
- **Roughness**: from mirror-smooth to matte.
- **Metallic**: how much it behaves like metal.
- **Clear Coat**: a glossy layer over the surface.
- **Transmission**: how much light passes through, for glass and clear plastics.
- For materials with a surface structure: **Grain**, **Grain Direction** and **Structure Scale**.

When you change one, the line under the name adds "Custom". Click the material's tile again to go back to the original.

## Good to know

- The **Tint** field only appears for materials that can be tinted. Photographed materials, such as the woods and stones, keep the colour they were photographed in.
- To give one face a material of its own, see [Materials for single faces](doc:visualize-faces).
- Each tile's name says its finish, for example "Linear brushed". Search for a finish word, such as brushed or satin, to find several at once.

> The finish of each body is kept with the project on this device. It is not part of the model file, so it does not travel when you share the project.

articles.title: Materials for single faces
articles.summary: Click a face to give it a material or a colour of its own; double-click for the body.
articles.keywords: face material colour color paint single face palette hex highlight stripe accent mark wood top two materials double click body
articles.body:
A face can have a material of its own: a wooden top on a metal box. The rest of the body keeps the body's material.

1. Point at the render. The face under the pointer lights up, as in Modeling.
2. Click a face. Shift-click adds more, and clicking the same single face again lets it go. **Apply to:** names it, for example "1 face of Body 1".
3. Choose a material in the library, or change the one **In Use**. It goes to the picked faces alone.
4. To give a face back to its body, pick it and press **Use the body's material**.

Double-click a body to pick all of it. A material chosen then goes to the whole body, except the faces that have one of their own: they keep theirs.

A face can also have just a colour on top of its material, from the row of nine under the picked faces, or from the rainbow circle at its end. **Use the body's colour** takes it off.

![](image:faces)

A face that is picked is tinted blue so that you can see it, which hides its true colour. Click empty space in the render to let go of all the picked faces and see the colours as they will render.

Faces keep their materials and colours through changes to the model, because faces are found by their stable names. They are kept with the project on this device.

## Related

- [Materials](doc:visualize-materials)
- [Visualize overview](doc:visualize)

articles.title: Lights and glowing materials
articles.summary: Make a body shine: LEDs, strips and a headlight that light the scene around them.
articles.keywords: light emission emissive led glow headlight spotlight area light strength beam angle lamp bloom luminous neon lit
articles.body:
The **Light** group of the material library holds materials that give off light: Warm LED, Cool LED, LED Strip, Warm LED Strip, Red LED, Green LED, Blue LED and Headlight.

1. Pick the body that is the light.
2. Search for the name, or find it in **Light**, and click it.
3. In **In Use**, open **Adjust** if it is folded, and set the controls.

![](image:controls)

- **Tint**: the colour of the light. Six suggested colours sit under the colour field.
- **Light Strength**: how bright, from 0 to 20 times. At 0 the body does not glow.
- **Light emission**: **Surface glow** only brightens the surface. **Area light** also lights the floor and other bodies. **Spotlight** casts a beam.
- **Direction**: for an area light or spotlight, which way it shines. The choices are Front · −Y, Back · +Y, Left · −X, Right · +X, Up · +Z and Down · −Z, along the model's axes.
- **Beam Angle**: for a spotlight, how wide the beam is, from 5 to 100 degrees.
- **Light Glow**: the halo around bright parts. It is the same setting as **Glow** in the [Camera tab](doc:visualize-camera).

The Headlight starts as a spotlight. The others start as area lights.

## Tips

- A light shows best in a dark studio, such as Technical Studio. See [Environment and light](doc:visualize-environment).
- If the light seems to point the wrong way, change **Direction**. The axes are the model's, not the view's.
- Lower **Light Strength** if the part washes out to white.

> Choosing an ordinary material takes the emission off the body again.

## Related

- [Materials](doc:visualize-materials)
- [Visualize overview](doc:visualize)

articles.title: Environment and light in Visualize
articles.summary: Choose a studio, then set the exposure, ambient light, key light angle and ground shadow.
articles.keywords: environment studio hdri backdrop background transparent exposure ambient key light angle ground shadow lighting neutral warm technical dark white
articles.body:
Open the **Environment** tab.

## Photographic Studio

Choose one of five set-ups:

- **Neutral Studio**: soft grey light and backdrop. It is the one a new project starts with.
- **Warm Studio**: a dark, warm room.
- **Technical Studio**: a cool, dark backdrop.
- **Custom Backdrop**: a plain colour of your own. A **Backdrop** colour field appears. It starts without a ground shadow.
- **Transparent**: no backdrop and no ground, so a capture can be placed on any page.

![](image:studios)

The first time a studio is used its lighting is loaded and filtered, so there is a short wait. A **Loading…** note shows while it works. If it cannot load, Visualize uses a plain light instead and says "The photographic studio could not load. Using fallback light."

## Light

- **Exposure**: overall brightness, from −2 to +2 EV.
- **Ambient**: how much light the studio gives, from 0 to 200 percent.
- **Key Light Angle**: turns the main light around the part, from −180 to 180 degrees. Use it to move the highlights and the shadow.
- **Ground Shadow**: a checkbox for the shadow under the part. It is off and greyed in the Transparent studio.

Choosing a studio sets these to values that suit it, so choose the studio first and adjust afterwards. Your material and camera choices are not touched.

## Tips

- A dark part reads best on a light backdrop, and a light part on a dark one.
- For a picture to place on a page with its own background, choose Transparent and press **Capture**. See [Capture](doc:visualize-render).

## Related

- [Materials](doc:visualize-materials)
- [Camera, focus and depth of field](doc:visualize-camera)
- [Visualize overview](doc:visualize)

articles.title: Camera, focus and depth of field
articles.summary: Set the field of view and the aperture, and right-click the model to focus on it.
articles.keywords: camera field of view fov aperture depth of field dof focus blur bokeh f-stop glow lens perspective turntable length
articles.body:
Open the **Camera** tab.

![](image:camera)

- **Field of View**: from 15 to 90 degrees. A narrow view looks flatter, like a long lens, and a wide one exaggerates depth.
- **Aperture**: **Off**, or ƒ1.4, ƒ2, ƒ2.8, ƒ4, ƒ5.6 or ƒ8. A smaller number blurs what is away from the focus more. A small drawing of five posts shows what will be sharp and what will be soft.
- **Focus Distance**: appears once an aperture is chosen. Move the focus nearer or farther. The line in the drawing moves with it.
- **Glow**: the halo around bright parts.
- **Turntable Length**: the seconds one turn takes, from 4 to 30. It sets the length of the [video](doc:visualize-render).

## Focus by clicking

Right-click a point on the model. The focus moves to it. If the aperture was off, it is set to ƒ2.8. This is quicker than the slider.

The blur is a photographic effect, so it only shows in the render and in a capture. Set the aperture to **Off** to see the whole part sharp again.

## Frame the part

**Frame** in the render bar fits the part into the view again after you have turned or zoomed.

## Related

- [Capture, turntable and video](doc:visualize-render)

articles.title: Decals: put a picture on the model
articles.summary: Place a PNG, JPEG or WebP image, such as a logo, on a surface of the part.
articles.keywords: decal image logo label sticker picture texture print png jpeg webp drop import brand marking
articles.body:
In the **Material** tab, find **Decal**. It sits between **In Use** and the library; press **Done** in **In Use** if you cannot see it.

1. Set the **Decal size**, in millimetres. It starts at 15, and the decal is a square of that size.
2. Drop an image file onto the model in the render. It is placed where you drop it.
3. Or press **Import…** and choose a file. It is placed at the centre of the view.

![](image:decal)

PNG, JPEG and WebP files work, up to 15 MB. A PNG with a transparent background is the best for a logo. A button, **Clear**, with the number of decals, removes them all.

## If it does not work

- "Drop the decal directly on the model." means the spot you dropped on is not on the part. Aim at the surface.
- "Use a PNG, JPEG or WebP under 15 MB." means the file is another type or too large.
- A decal placed near an edge can be cut off or bent around it. Use a smaller size, or aim at the middle of a flat face.

> Decals are placed in the render only. They are not saved with the project, and they are cleared when the model changes or you leave Visualize. Press **Capture** to keep a picture of them.

## Related

- [Capture, turntable and video](doc:visualize-render)
- [Materials](doc:visualize-materials)
- [Visualize overview](doc:visualize)

articles.title: Capture a picture, turntable and video
articles.summary: Save the render as a PNG, turn the part, or record one full turn as a video.
articles.keywords: capture screenshot png image export render turntable video record 360 webm mp4 frame save picture animation spin rotate
articles.body:
The render bar is at the top of Visualize.

![](image:bar)

- **Capture**: saves the render as **bezier-render.png**. It is greyed until the renderer is ready.
- **Turntable**: turns the part slowly. The button becomes **Stop Turntable**.
- **Record 360°**: records exactly one turn and saves it when it ends. Press **Stop & Save Video** to finish early. The file is **bezier-turntable.webm**, or .mp4 in a browser that makes only that. The turn takes as long as **Turntable Length** in the [Camera tab](doc:visualize-camera), 12 seconds to start with.
- **Frame**: fits the part to the view.

Because the video is exactly one turn, it ends on the frame it began on and loops cleanly.

In a browser the file goes to your downloads folder. In the desktop app a save dialog asks where.

## Before you capture

1. Choose the material and the studio.
2. Turn and zoom the part to the view you want, then wait a moment for the render to settle.
3. Press **Capture**. If the picture comes back empty, Visualize says "The capture came back empty. Try again once the render has settled."

> If the browser cannot record video, Visualize says "Video recording is not available in this browser" and the button does nothing. Capture still works.

## Related

- [Environment and light](doc:visualize-environment)
- [Camera, focus and depth of field](doc:visualize-camera)

articles.title: Measure the distance between two points
articles.summary: Click two points on the model to read the straight-line distance, and pin it.
articles.keywords: measure measurement distance ruler dimension length point to point delta xyz inspect check pin copy how long how far size tape
articles.body:
Measure reads a length off the model. It never changes it.

## Take a measurement

1. Press **Measure** at the foot of the left rail, in Modeling. A **Measure** panel opens, with the steps **First point** and **Second point**.
2. Move over a face. Dots show the points a click can land on: its corners and its middle.
3. Click the first point, then the second. A line is drawn between them.
4. The **Distance** appears in the panel, in the unit you have chosen for the project (Units & Grid in the quick settings).

![](image:panel)

Click the number to copy it. It is on its way to a field or a message most of the time, so it is a button.

## Axis distances

Switch on **Include X, Y, Z deltas** to see how much of the distance lies along each axis.

## Keep it

- **Pin measurement** keeps the reading drawn on the model after you leave Measure. The panel lists pinned readings; **×** removes one.
- **New measurement**, or **Clear**, starts again without leaving the tool.
- **Exit Measure**, the **×** of the panel, closes it. Esc does the same.

Pinned readings go away when the model changes or the project closes, because their points are positions in space and not parts of the model.

## Moving the panel

Drag the grip at the top of the panel. With the grip focused, the arrow keys move it by 10 pixels, and with Shift by 40.

## Good to know

- It measures between points, not along an edge or around a curve. For the size of something you are building, a [dimension](doc:dimensions) in the sketch is the better tool.
- Measure is not in the Simulation rail. Switching workspace leaves it.
- Choosing a modeling tool leaves Measure. Pinned readings stay on screen.

panel.alt: The Measure panel with a distance and its X, Y, Z deltas, and the line it measures on the box

articles.title: Section View: look inside the model
articles.summary: Cut the view with a horizontal plane to see what is inside, without changing the model.
articles.keywords: section view cut clip plane slice inside cross section inspect hide above z height cutaway
articles.body:
Section View hides the part of the model above a horizontal plane, so you can see inside. It is for looking only: the geometry is not cut. The cut is closed over with a hatched face, as a section is drawn on paper, so you can tell material from air.

## Use it

1. Press **Section View** in the left rail, at the bottom, in Modeling. The rail button then reads **On**, and a panel opens. The plane starts through the middle of the model.
2. Set its height in the **Z position** field. Type a number and press Enter, or drag the number up and down.
3. Press **Center on model** to put the plane through the middle again, or **Reset to origin** to put it at zero.
4. Press the rail button again, or close the panel, to leave.

![](image:panel)

## The field

- Dragging moves the plane half a millimetre for each pixel. A click without moving lets you type.
- A value that is not a number is marked and not applied. Esc puts the old value back.
- The unit is the one set for the project.
- Only horizontal cuts exist: the plane is always parallel to the XY plane. To look from the side instead, use the [standard views](doc:standard-views).

> The model is unchanged and so are your exports. While you measure, the section's panel is hidden and the cut stays; leave Measure to bring the panel back. Section View exists only on screen. For a cut in a technical drawing, see [section A–A](doc:drawings-views).

panel.alt: The Section View panel with a cut through a box

articles.title: Learn: lessons you can watch and follow
articles.summary: The Learn page keeps your lessons, filters them by level and picks up where you left off.
articles.keywords: learn lessons tutorial course video beginner intermediate advanced level import export bezierlesson continue progress completed training
articles.body:
A lesson is a recording of someone building a part in Bezier, with the model saved at each step. You can watch it, or follow along in the editor.

## Open Learn

Open the start page with the house button and choose **Learn** in the sidebar.

![](image:page)

## The page

- **Level**: a switch with **All**, **Beginner**, **Intermediate** and **Advanced**. It appears once you have a lesson. While it or the search is narrowing the list, the count reads, for example, "1 of 3 lessons" and the Continue card is left out.
- **Import…** and **Record**: bring in a lesson file, or [make a lesson](doc:learn-record).
- **Continue**: if you left a lesson part-way, a wide card at the top offers to pick up where you stopped, with its chapter and time.
- **The cards**: a picture of each lesson, its length, level and number of chapters. A check mark means you finished it. A thin line under the picture shows how far you got.

The search field of the start page filters the lessons by their words. If none fit, the page says "No lessons match."

## Open a lesson

Click a card to [watch it](doc:learn-player). Hover over a card to see a short silent preview. The **⋯** button, or a right-click, offers:

- **Play**
- **Follow Along in the Editor**: see [follow a lesson](doc:learn-follow)
- **Export…**: saves the lesson as a **.bezierlesson** file to share
- **Delete…**: asks first

## Get a lesson

- Drop a **.bezierlesson** file anywhere on the page, or press **Import…**. You can choose several files at once. One file opens in the player when it is in; several are added and the page says so.
- On the alpha channel, download one from [Community](doc:community). It appears here.
- Record your own.

With no lessons the page says "No lessons yet" and offers **Import a lesson…** and **Record one**.

If a file cannot be read, a notice says which file it was. Nothing is added.

To watch or follow a lesson next, see [watch a lesson](doc:learn-player) and [follow a lesson](doc:learn-follow).

## Your lesson projects

When you follow a lesson and build the model yourself, the model is kept under **Your Lesson Projects**, below the lessons. They open like projects, with the lesson beside them. They are not in the list of [projects](doc:projects).

page.alt: The Learn page with its level switch, the Import and Record buttons and a lesson card

articles.title: Watch a lesson
articles.summary: Play, scrub, jump between chapters, change speed and use the keyboard.
articles.keywords: lesson player watch play pause chapters speed repeat fullscreen keyboard shortcuts completed mark progress
articles.body:
Click a lesson card to open its player.

![](image:player)

## The player

- The recording of the editor fills the stage. Double-click it for full screen.
- The **chapters** are listed beside it. Click one to jump to it.
- Under the video: **Play**, **Previous chapter**, **Next chapter**, the time, **Playback speed**, **Mute** and **Full screen**. The **Repeat this chapter** and **Keyboard shortcuts** buttons are here too.
- Parts the author cut out are skipped.

Along the top: **Follow along**, **Edit Lesson**, and a **More** menu with **Mark as completed**, **Export…** and **Delete…**. A lesson is marked completed when it plays to the end. Where you stopped is remembered, and Learn offers it under Continue.

## Keys

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| **Space**, **K** | Play or pause |
| **J**, **L** | Back or forward 10 seconds |
| **←**, **→** | Back or forward 5 seconds |
| **↑**, **↓** or **P**, **N** | Previous or next chapter |
| **0** to **9** | Jump to a tenth of the lesson |
| **Home**, **End** | Start or end |
| **R** | Repeat this chapter |
| **M** | Mute |
| **F** | Full screen |
| **?** | Show the list of keys |

player.alt: The lesson player with its chapters and controls

articles.title: Follow a lesson in the editor
articles.summary: Keep the lesson in a small window over the editor while the model follows the video.
articles.keywords: follow along lesson pip picture in picture checkpoint model follows video leave resize fold lesson project save
articles.body:
1. Open a lesson and press **Follow along**, or choose **Follow Along in the Editor** in a card's menu.
2. The editor opens with the lesson in a small window over it. The model shows the lesson's checkpoint for the part of the video that is playing.
3. Play the lesson, and build the same thing yourself. To go back over a step, press the previous chapter button. While **The model follows the video** is ticked, the model goes back with it.

![](image:panel)

## The window

- Drag its header to move it. It sticks to the edges. With the grip focused, the arrow keys move it.
- Drag a corner to resize it, or scroll over the video to make it larger or smaller.
- **Make the video larger** gives the video the room, and **Make the editor larger** gives it back. **V** does the same.
- While the window is open, **Space** or **K** plays and pauses, **←** and **→** move 5 seconds, and **↑** and **↓** change chapter. Keys are ignored while you type in a field.
- **Fold the lesson away** keeps only a play button and the chapter name. **Show the lesson** opens it again.
- **Leave** ends it and pauses the video.

If the lesson was recorded with the author's camera, there is a second picture of them. Press its edge to swap which is larger.

## The model and you

**The model follows the video** is ticked at the start. As soon as you make a change of your own, it unticks, so the lesson stops replacing your work. Tick it again to see the lesson's checkpoint.

What you build is saved as a lesson project. Find it on [Learn](doc:learn), under Your Lesson Projects. Its menu has **Save as Project** to put a copy among your normal [projects](doc:projects).

panel.alt: A lesson in a small window over the editor

articles.title: Record and edit a lesson
articles.summary: Record the editor, add checkpoints, then cut, name chapters and export.
articles.keywords: record lesson recording author create tutorial microphone camera checkpoint chapters trim cut zoom edit export share
articles.body:
## Record

1. On [Learn](doc:learn), press **Record**.
2. Give it a **Title**, choose a **Level**, and tick **Microphone** or **Your camera, in a corner** if you want them.
3. If a project is open, choose to record in **An empty model** or **The open project**.
4. Press **Start recording**. The editor opens.

![](image:sheet)

A bar shows the time. **Pause** and **Resume** stop it for a while. **Checkpoint** keeps the model as it is, as a chapter. **Finish** ends the recording. Paused, **Discard…** throws it away.

The recording takes the editor's view, your keys and clicks, and a checkpoint of the model after every change.

> Recording needs a browser that can record the view. If this one cannot, the sheet says so. If the app reloads in the middle, Learn offers to keep or discard what was saved.

## Edit

When you finish, the edit view opens.

- Under the picture is a timeline of clips, chapters and zooms. Space plays it.
- **I** and **O** set an in and an out point. **Cut between** hides that stretch from learners. The recording keeps it, and **Restore** brings it back.
- **C** splits a clip at the playhead. **M** adds a chapter there, and you can name each chapter in the list.
- **Zoom in between** (**Z**) zooms the recording for that stretch.
- **About this lesson** holds the title, description and level.
- If you recorded your camera, choose its corner from the playhead on.
- **Undo** and **Redo** work on these edits, and they are saved as you go.

Press **Export…** to save a **.bezierlesson** file, and **Done** to go back to the player.

sheet.alt: The Record sheet with title, level and options

articles.title: Open Settings
articles.summary: How to reach Settings, and what each of its pages is for.
articles.keywords: settings preferences options configuration open gear cog menu pages sections search find setting where is preferences dialog customise customize
articles.body:
Settings lives on the start page, at the foot of the sidebar. It is a place you visit, not one you work in.

![](image:sidebar)

## Open it

- From the start page, click **Settings** at the bottom of the sidebar.
- From the editor, press {{key:settings}}. Settings opens over the start page.
- Press the same key again, or Escape, to close it. If you came from the editor, you go back to the editor.

## Find a setting by name

Click the **Search** field of the start page, or press **/**, and type a word: `theme`, `trackpad`, `shortcut`. The settings that hold it are listed under your projects. Click one to open its page.

![](image:search)

Type `settings:` first to look only through the settings, for example `settings: theme`. Inside Settings, the list on the left then shows only the pages that match.

Changes apply as you make them. There is no Save button. They are kept on this device, in this browser. If the browser blocks its storage, as a private window may, the changes hold until you close the page.

## The pages

![](image:pages)

The pages are listed in groups on the left.

- **Bezier.** [General](doc:settings-general): the workspace projects open in and a few interface switches. [Appearance](doc:settings-appearance): theme, contrast, glass, density, size and motion. [Nib](doc:settings-nib): the robot at the top of the window, and his lessons.
- **Workspace.** Interaction: mouse and trackpad, see [orbit, pan and zoom](doc:navigate). [Viewport](doc:settings-viewport): how finely curves are drawn, and how the view behaves while it moves. [Shortcuts](doc:settings-shortcuts): the key for every command.
- **Sharing.** Collaboration and Community, on the alpha channel only. See [collaboration](doc:collaboration) and [community](doc:community).
- **System.** [Updates](doc:settings-updates): the installed version, and the channel: stable, beta or alpha. [MCP & Automation](doc:settings-mcp): let an assistant such as Claude connect, and see what it did. [Data & Privacy](doc:settings-data): what is stored, and a reset for the settings.
- **Make it better.** [Contribute](doc:settings-contribute): report a problem, suggest something, or read the code.

## Which page for what

| You want to | Go to |
| --- | --- |
| A darker or lighter interface, larger text, calmer animation | [Appearance](doc:settings-appearance) |
| Curves that look faceted, or a large model that turns roughly | [Viewport](doc:settings-viewport) |
| The keys of another CAD program, or a different key for one command | [Shortcuts](doc:settings-shortcuts) |
| The mouse and trackpad to move the camera the way you are used to | [Orbit, pan and zoom](doc:navigate) |
| A frame-rate readout in the top bar | [General](doc:settings-general) |
| Every setting back to how it came | [Data & Privacy](doc:settings-data) |

articles.title: Settings: General
articles.summary: Choose the workspace new projects open in, and switch a few interface extras on or off.
articles.keywords: general startup workspace default modeling visualize drawings performance graph fps frame rate frame time lag slow labels tool labels rail names history references
articles.body:
Settings, General has three groups. Open it from [Settings](doc:open-settings).

![](image:page)

## Startup

**Open new projects in** chooses the workspace a project opens in: Modeling, Visualize or Drawings. Modeling is the default. It is used the next time a project opens. You can change workspace at any time, see [workspaces](doc:workspaces).

## Interface

![](image:interface)

- **Show performance graph** puts a small live readout in the top bar. Off by default. A right click anywhere on the top bar of the editor switches it on or off as well. It shows one timing at a time: frame time, frame cadence or main-thread delay, with a trace of the last seconds. Scroll over it, press an arrow key or click it to turn to the next. Use it when a large model feels slow, and for nothing else.
- **Show tool labels** keeps the names beside the rail buttons. On by default. Switch it off for a narrower rail. The names are also left out while a tool column is open beside the left rail.

![](image:graph)

> To put every setting back, see [Data & Privacy](doc:settings-data). For how the view draws a large model, see [Viewport](doc:settings-viewport).

interface.alt: The Startup and Interface groups, with the performance graph switch

graph.alt: The performance graph in the top bar of the editor, beside the workspace menu

articles.title: Settings: Appearance
articles.summary: Set the theme, contrast, glass effect, panel density, interface size and motion.
articles.keywords: appearance theme dark light system mode contrast glass blur transparency density compact size scale font text zoom motion animation reduced accessibility
articles.body:
Settings, Appearance changes how the interface looks. It does not change the model.

![](image:page)

## Color

- **Theme**: System, Light or Dark. System follows your computer.
- **Contrast**: Standard or High. High makes text and the lines between panels brighter.
- **Selection**: the one colour for everything you pick: faces, edges, bodies and sketch lines, in Modeling and Visualize, and the marks around them such as the move handle.

## Materials

![](image:materials)

- **Glass**: Full, Reduced or Solid. The panels are frosted glass over the model. Reduced blurs less and is more opaque. Solid has no blur at all, which is the lightest on a slow computer.
- **Panel density**: Comfortable or Compact. Compact makes the spacing smaller and the rail buttons shorter, so more fits on a small screen.
- **Interface size**: 90%, 100% or 110%. This sets the size of the text in the interface.

## Motion

**Interface motion**: System, Reduced or Full. System follows the reduced-motion setting of your computer. Reduced shortens animations and transitions to nothing. Full keeps them even if your computer asks for less.

Every choice applies at once and is kept. To undo all of them, see [Data & Privacy](doc:settings-data).

> A slow computer gains most from **Solid** glass and, in [Viewport](doc:settings-viewport), **Performance** surface quality.
